facts.ja: 太陽の表面温度は約5500℃だが、外側の大気（コロナ）は100万℃以上になる。その理由はまだ完全には解明されていない。
facts.easy: The surface of the sun is about 5,500°C. But the air around it is over one million degrees. Scientists still do not fully know why.
facts.std: The Sun's surface is about 5,500°C, yet its outer atmosphere, the corona, exceeds a million degrees. Why the corona is so much hotter is still not fully understood.

facts.ja: 光が太陽から地球に届くまで約8分20秒かかる。今見えている太陽は約8分前の姿。
facts.easy: Light from the sun takes about eight minutes to reach us. So the sun we see is the sun of eight minutes ago.
facts.std: Sunlight takes about 8 minutes and 20 seconds to reach Earth, so we always see the Sun as it was a little over eight minutes earlier.

facts.ja: 観測できる宇宙には数千億〜2兆個の銀河があると推定されている。天の川銀河だけでも1000億〜4000億個の星がある。
facts.easy: There may be hundreds of billions of groups of stars in space. Our own group has more than 100 billion stars.
facts.std: Estimates suggest the observable universe holds hundreds of billions, perhaps up to two trillion, galaxies. The Milky Way alone contains 100 to 400 billion stars.

facts.ja: 土星の平均密度は水より低い。理屈の上では、土星が入るほど巨大な海があれば浮かぶ。
facts.easy: Saturn is lighter than water for its size. If there were a sea big enough, Saturn could float in it.
facts.std: Saturn's average density is lower than that of water, so in theory it would float in an ocean large enough to hold it.

facts.ja: 月は毎年約3.8cmずつ地球から遠ざかっている。数億年後には皆既日食が起きなくなると考えられている。
facts.easy: The moon moves about 3.8 cm away from us every year. In a few hundred million years, it will be too far to fully cover the sun.
facts.std: The Moon drifts about 3.8 cm farther from Earth each year. In several hundred million years it will appear too small to cause total solar eclipses.

facts.ja: 木星の大赤斑は地球より大きな巨大な嵐で、少なくとも150年以上観測され続けている。
facts.easy: Jupiter has a giant storm that is bigger than the Earth. People have watched it for more than 150 years.
facts.std: Jupiter's Great Red Spot is a storm wider than Earth that has been observed continuously for more than 150 years.

facts.ja: 宇宙の年齢は約138億年。地球の年齢（約46億年）の約3倍にあたる。
facts.easy: The universe is about 13.8 billion years old. That is about three times as old as the Earth.
facts.std: The universe is roughly 13.8 billion years old, about three times the age of Earth, which formed around 4.6 billion years ago.

facts.ja: 中性子星は太陽より重い質量を直径20km程度に押し込めた星。ティースプーン1杯分で約10億トンになる。
facts.easy: A neutron star is heavier than the sun but only about 20 km wide. One small spoon of it would weigh about a billion tons.
facts.std: A neutron star packs more mass than the Sun into a sphere about 20 km across. A teaspoon of its material would weigh around a billion tons.

facts.ja: 金星の1日（自転にかかる243日）は1年（公転225日）より長い。しかも金星では太陽が西から昇る。
facts.easy: On Venus, one day is longer than one year. And the sun comes up in the west.
facts.std: Venus takes 243 Earth days to spin once but only 225 to orbit the Sun, so its day is longer than its year. It also spins backward, so the Sun rises in the west.

facts.ja: 国際宇宙ステーション（ISS）は約90分で地球を1周するため、1日に16回ほど日の出と日の入りを見られる。
facts.easy: The space station goes around the Earth in about 90 minutes. People on it can see about 16 sunrises a day.
facts.std: The International Space Station circles Earth roughly every 90 minutes, so its crew sees about 16 sunrises and sunsets every day.

facts.ja: ダイヤモンドも鉛筆の芯（黒鉛）も同じ炭素でできている。違うのは原子の並び方だけ。
facts.easy: Diamonds and pencil lead are both made of carbon. The only difference is how the tiny parts are lined up.
facts.std: Diamond and the graphite in pencils are both pure carbon. They differ only in how their atoms are arranged.

facts.ja: 雪の結晶は、まったく同じ形のものはまずないと考えられている。成長中の温度や湿度のわずかな違いで形が変わるため。
facts.easy: It is very likely that no two snowflakes are the same. Small changes in the air change their shape as they grow.
facts.std: It is extremely unlikely for two snowflakes to be identical, because tiny differences in temperature and humidity shape each crystal as it grows.

facts.ja: 虹は本当は円の形をしているが、地面にさえぎられて半円に見える。飛行機から見ると丸い虹が見えることがある。
facts.easy: A rainbow is really a full circle. We only see half because the ground is in the way. From a plane, you can sometimes see the whole circle.
facts.std: Rainbows are actually full circles; the ground hides the lower half. From an aircraft you can sometimes see a complete circular rainbow.

facts.ja: 雷の通り道は約3万℃近くになり、太陽の表面の約5倍熱い。ただしその熱はほんの一瞬しか続かない。
facts.easy: Lightning can be about five times hotter than the surface of the sun. But the heat lasts for only a moment.
facts.std: A lightning channel can reach nearly 30,000°C, about five times hotter than the Sun's surface, but only for a fraction of a second.

facts.ja: 鳥や魚、昆虫の中には地球の磁場を使って方角を知るものがいる。その感じ取る仕組みは完全には解明されていない。
facts.easy: Some birds, fish and insects use the Earth's magnetic field to find their way. We still do not fully know how they feel it.
facts.std: Many birds, fish and insects navigate using Earth's magnetic field, but exactly how they sense it is still not fully understood.

facts.ja: 「シュレーディンガーの猫」は、量子の世界の不思議さを示すための思考実験。箱を開けるまで猫の状態が決まらないという話で有名。
facts.easy: Schrödinger's cat is a famous story about a cat in a box. It shows how strange the world of very small things can be.
facts.std: Schrödinger's cat is a thought experiment about a cat in a sealed box, created to show how strange quantum mechanics seems when applied to everyday objects.

facts.ja: 絶対零度（−273.15℃）は理論上の最低温度。物質はこれ以上冷やせず、分子の動きは最も小さい状態になる。
facts.easy: The lowest possible temperature is minus 273.15°C. Nothing can be colder than this.
facts.std: Absolute zero, minus 273.15°C, is the lowest temperature possible. At this point particles have the least motion that physics allows.

facts.ja: 光の速さ（秒速約30万km）は、宇宙で情報や物が進める最高の速さとされる（特殊相対性理論）。
facts.easy: Light moves about 300,000 km in one second. Nothing can travel faster than light.
facts.std: Light travels about 300,000 km per second, and according to special relativity nothing that carries information can go faster.

facts.ja: 地球は完全な球ではなく、少しつぶれた形をしている。赤道の半径は北極・南極までの半径より約21km長い。
facts.easy: The Earth is not a perfect ball. It is a little wider around the middle, by about 21 km.
facts.std: Earth is not a perfect sphere but slightly flattened; its radius at the equator is about 21 km longer than at the poles.

facts.ja: 太陽は毎秒約6億トンの水素をヘリウムに変えている。この核融合が光と熱を生み出す。
facts.easy: Every second, the sun changes about 600 million tons of one gas into another. This gives us light and heat.
facts.std: Every second the Sun fuses about 600 million tonnes of hydrogen into helium, and this nuclear fusion produces its light and heat.

facts.ja: 流れ星の正体は、砂粒ほどの小さなちり。大気に飛び込んで高温になり、光りながら燃えつきる。
facts.easy: A shooting star is often just a small piece of dust. It burns up as it falls into the air around the Earth.
facts.std: Most shooting stars are specks of dust no bigger than a grain of sand that burn up as they plunge into Earth's atmosphere.

facts.ja: 水は凍ると液体のときより軽くなる（密度が下がる）めずらしい物質。だから氷は水に浮き、湖は底まで凍りにくい。
facts.easy: Ice is lighter than water, which is very unusual. That is why ice floats and lakes do not freeze all the way down.
facts.std: Unusually, water becomes less dense when it freezes. That is why ice floats and why lakes rarely freeze solid from top to bottom.

facts.ja: 水が100℃で沸騰するのは海面の高さでの話。エベレストの山頂では約70℃で沸騰する。
facts.easy: Water boils at 100°C near the sea. On top of Mount Everest, it boils at about 70°C.
facts.std: Water boils at 100°C only at sea level. At the summit of Mount Everest, where the air pressure is low, it boils at about 70°C.

facts.ja: 空気にも重さがある。1立方メートルの空気は約1.2kgで、ふつうの部屋の空気は大人1人分くらいの重さになる。
facts.easy: Air has weight. The air in a normal room can weigh about as much as one adult.
facts.std: Air has weight: one cubic meter weighs about 1.2 kg, so the air in an ordinary room can weigh as much as an adult person.

facts.ja: タコには心臓が3つあり、血は青い。銅を含むヘモシアニンという物質が酸素を運ぶため。
facts.easy: An octopus has three hearts and blue blood.
facts.std: An octopus has three hearts and blue blood, because its oxygen is carried by a copper-based protein called hemocyanin.

facts.ja: チーターは時速100kmを超える速さで走れるが、全力で走れるのは数十秒ほど。
facts.easy: A cheetah can run faster than 100 km an hour. But it can only run that fast for a short time.
facts.std: Cheetahs can sprint at over 100 km per hour, but only for a short burst of a few hundred meters.

facts.ja: フラミンゴのひなは灰色っぽい白で生まれる。エサに含まれるカロテノイドという色素で、だんだんピンクになる。
facts.easy: Baby flamingos are not pink. They become pink from the food they eat.
facts.std: Flamingo chicks hatch grey-white. They turn pink gradually thanks to carotenoid pigments in the algae and shrimp they eat.

facts.ja: ゾウはジャンプができない。体が重く脚の作りの関係で、4本の脚が同時に地面から離れることがない。
facts.easy: Elephants cannot jump. They are too heavy, and they always keep at least one foot on the ground.
facts.std: Elephants cannot jump. Because of their weight and leg structure, they always keep at least one foot on the ground, even when moving fast.

facts.ja: ハチの巣の六角形は、少ない材料で広い空間を作れる効率のよい形。数学的にも最も効率がよいことが証明されている。
facts.easy: Bees build their homes with six-sided rooms. This shape uses the least material to make the most space.
facts.std: The hexagons of a honeycomb divide space using the least amount of wall material, something mathematicians proved in 1999.

facts.ja: カメレオンは左右の目を別々に動かせて、ほぼ360度を見渡せる。体の色は、気分や温度、仲間への合図で変わる。
facts.easy: A chameleon can move each eye on its own and see almost all around. Its color changes with its mood and the temperature.
facts.std: A chameleon can move each eye independently to see nearly all around it. Its color shifts mainly with mood, temperature and signals to other chameleons.

facts.ja: サメの骨格は骨ではなく軟骨でできているため、化石に残りにくい。そのかわり歯の化石はたくさん見つかっている。
facts.easy: A shark's body is not held up by hard bone. So shark bodies rarely last as fossils, but many of their teeth do.
facts.std: Shark skeletons are made of cartilage rather than bone, so they seldom fossilize, while their teeth are found in huge numbers.

facts.ja: アリは自分の体重の何十倍もの重さを運ぶことができる。
facts.easy: An ant can carry things many times heavier than its own body.
facts.std: Ants can carry loads many times their own body weight, sometimes up to around fifty times.

facts.ja: クジラの低い鳴き声は、海の中を数千kmも伝わることがある。
facts.easy: The low calls of some whales can travel thousands of kilometers under the sea.
facts.std: The low-frequency calls of large whales such as blue and fin whales can travel thousands of kilometers through the ocean.

facts.ja: カラスは人の顔を見分けて覚えられる。いやなことをした人を何年も覚えていて、仲間にも伝えることがある。
facts.easy: Crows can remember human faces. They can remember a bad person for years and even tell other crows.
facts.std: Crows can recognize individual human faces, remember people who threatened them for years, and even pass the warning to other crows.

facts.ja: 猫のひげは周りを感じ取るセンサー。すき間を通れるかを判断したり、暗い所で動いたりするのに役立つ。
facts.easy: A cat uses its whiskers to feel the world. They help it know if it can fit through a small space.
facts.std: A cat's whiskers are sensitive touch sensors that help it judge narrow gaps and move around in the dark.

facts.ja: 地球には約3兆本の木があると推定されている。人間1人あたり約400本にあたる。
facts.easy: There are about three trillion trees on the Earth. That is about 400 trees for each person.
facts.std: Researchers estimate there are about three trillion trees on Earth, roughly 400 for every person.

facts.ja: カタツムリには歯があり、種類によっては舌の上に何万本もの小さな歯が並んでいる。やすりのように食べ物を削る。
facts.easy: Snails have teeth. Some have thousands of very small teeth on their tongue.
facts.std: Snails have a tongue-like ribbon covered in rows of tiny teeth, called a radula; some species have many thousands of them.

facts.ja: ライオンのたてがみが黒っぽいほど、オスとして強いしるしになり、メスに好まれるという研究がある。
facts.easy: A study found that female lions like males with darker hair around the head.
facts.std: Research in Tanzania found that lions with darker manes tend to be healthier and are preferred by females.

facts.ja: ペンギンは空を飛べないが、水中では時速30km以上で泳げる種類もいる。翼がひれのように進化した。
facts.easy: Penguins cannot fly, but some can swim more than 30 km an hour. Their wings work like flippers.
facts.std: Penguins cannot fly, but their wings have evolved into flippers, and some species can swim at over 30 km per hour.

facts.ja: アイスランドガイという二枚貝には500年以上生きた個体が見つかっている。知られている中で最も長生きの動物のひとつ。
facts.easy: A kind of sea animal with a shell was found to be over 500 years old.
facts.std: An ocean quahog clam found off Iceland was more than 500 years old, making it one of the longest-lived animals ever recorded.

facts.ja: チョウの幼虫はさなぎの中で体の大部分がどろどろに溶け、残った細胞のかたまりから新しい体が作られる。
facts.easy: Inside the hard case, much of a young butterfly's body turns to liquid. Then a new body is built.
facts.std: Inside the chrysalis, much of a caterpillar's body breaks down into a soup, and small groups of cells then build the adult butterfly.

facts.ja: イルカは鏡に映った自分を自分だと分かる。この能力が確かめられている動物は、ヒト・大型類人猿・ゾウなど、ごくわずか。
facts.easy: Dolphins know themselves in a mirror. Very few animals can do this.
facts.std: Dolphins can recognize themselves in a mirror, an ability shown in only a few animals, such as humans, great apes and elephants.

facts.ja: 深海の生き物の多くは自分で光を出す（生物発光）。仲間との合図、えさを誘う、身を守るなどに使う。
facts.easy: Many animals deep in the sea make their own light. They use it to talk, to catch food and to stay safe.
facts.std: Many deep-sea creatures produce their own light, using bioluminescence to signal, attract prey and defend themselves.

facts.ja: ミツバチ1匹が一生のうちに作るハチミツは、ティースプーンの12分の1ほど。
facts.easy: In its whole life, one bee makes only a very small amount of honey, about one twelfth of a small spoon.
facts.std: A single worker honeybee produces only about one twelfth of a teaspoon of honey in its entire life.

facts.ja: 植物は、干ばつなどのストレスを経験すると、次のストレスにすばやく反応するようになることがある。「植物の記憶」として研究されている。
facts.easy: Some plants seem to remember dry times. After one dry time, they get ready faster for the next.
facts.std: Some plants that survive drought respond faster to the next one, a phenomenon researchers study as 'plant stress memory'.

facts.ja: ナマケモノは動きがとてもゆっくりなので、毛に藻が生え、そこにガが住むこともある。
facts.easy: Sloths move so slowly that green plants grow in their hair. Small insects even live there.
facts.std: Sloths move so slowly that algae grow in their fur, and moths live there too, forming a tiny ecosystem.

facts.ja: ワニの仲間は恐竜の時代から続く古いグループで、体のつくりは大昔からあまり変わっていない。
facts.easy: Crocodiles lived at the same time as dinosaurs. Their bodies have not changed much since then.
facts.std: Crocodilians are an ancient group that lived alongside the dinosaurs, and their basic body plan has changed little since then.

facts.ja: オウムの中には、言葉をまねるだけでなく、色や数を答えるなど意味を理解して使える個体もいた。
facts.easy: Some parrots do more than copy words. One parrot could name colors and count objects.
facts.std: Some parrots do more than mimic: a grey parrot named Alex could name colors, shapes and numbers of objects.

facts.ja: タコは眠っている間に体の色が変わることが観察されていて、夢のような状態があるのではないかと考えられている。
facts.easy: An octopus can change color while it sleeps. Some scientists think it may be dreaming.
facts.std: Sleeping octopuses have been filmed changing color, and some scientists think they may experience something like dreaming.

facts.ja: アメリカの「パンド」は、根でつながった1本のポプラの仲間の群れ。何千年も生きている、地球最古級の生物のひとつ。
facts.easy: Pando is a big group of trees in the United States. All the trees share one root and it is thousands of years old.
facts.std: Pando, a grove of quaking aspen in Utah, is a single organism connected by one root system and is thought to be thousands of years old.

facts.ja: エジプトでピラミッドが作られていたころ、北極海の島ではまだマンモスが生きていた。
facts.easy: When the pyramids were being built in Egypt, some mammoths were still alive on an island in the far north.
facts.std: When the Great Pyramid was built in Egypt, woolly mammoths still survived on Wrangel Island in the Arctic Ocean.

facts.ja: クレオパトラは、ピラミッドが作られた時代よりも、人類が月に行った時代のほうに近い時代の人。
facts.easy: Cleopatra lived closer in time to the moon landing than to the building of the Great Pyramid.
facts.std: Cleopatra lived closer in time to the Moon landing than to the construction of the Great Pyramid of Giza.

facts.ja: バイキングはコロンブスより約500年早く北アメリカに着いていた。カナダのランス・オ・メドーに遺跡が残る。
facts.easy: The Vikings reached North America about 500 years before Columbus.
facts.std: Norse explorers reached North America around the year 1000, about 500 years before Columbus, as the site at L'Anse aux Meadows in Canada shows.

facts.ja: モンゴル帝国は最大で約2400万km²を支配した、歴史上最大の陸続きの帝国。
facts.easy: The Mongol Empire was the biggest land empire in history.
facts.std: At its height, the Mongol Empire covered about 24 million square kilometers, the largest connected land empire in history.

facts.ja: ナポレオンの身長は約169cmで、当時のフランス人の平均よりやや高かった。「小柄」というイメージはイギリスの風刺画の影響が大きい。
facts.easy: Napoleon was about 169 cm tall. That was a little taller than most French men at the time.
facts.std: Napoleon was about 169 cm tall, slightly above the average for Frenchmen of his day; his 'short' image owes much to British cartoons.

facts.ja: コロンブスが1492年に最初に着いたのはアメリカ大陸ではなく、バハマ諸島の島だった。
facts.easy: In 1492, Columbus did not land on the big land of America. He landed on a small island in the Bahamas.
facts.std: On his first voyage in 1492, Columbus landed not on the American mainland but on an island in the Bahamas.

facts.ja: 江戸時代は約260年続き、大きな戦争のない時代が長く続いた。その間に日本独自の文化が育った。
facts.easy: The Edo period in Japan lasted about 260 years with no big wars. Many arts grew during that time.
facts.std: Japan's Edo period lasted about 260 years with no major wars, allowing a distinctive culture of art, theater and literature to flourish.

facts.ja: チョコレートの元になるカカオは、16世紀にスペイン人がアメリカ大陸から持ち帰るまでヨーロッパにはなかった。
facts.easy: There was no chocolate in Europe until the Spanish brought it from America in the 1500s.
facts.std: Chocolate was unknown in Europe until Spanish explorers brought cacao back from the Americas in the 16th century.

facts.ja: モナ・リザは、ルーブル美術館に展示される前、フランス王フランソワ1世の宮殿の浴室に飾られていた。
facts.easy: Before it went to a museum, the Mona Lisa hung in a king's bathroom.
facts.std: Before entering the Louvre, the Mona Lisa hung in the bathing rooms of King Francis I's palace at Fontainebleau.

facts.ja: 古代ギリシャのオリンピック（紀元前776年〜）では、選手は裸で競技していた。
facts.easy: In the first Olympic Games in Greece, the players took part with no clothes on.
facts.std: In the ancient Olympic Games, which began in 776 BC, athletes competed naked.

facts.ja: マリー・キュリーはノーベル賞を2回（物理学賞と化学賞）受けた最初の人。異なる2つの科学分野で受賞したのは今も彼女だけ。
facts.easy: Marie Curie was the first person to win the Nobel Prize two times.
facts.std: Marie Curie was the first person to win two Nobel Prizes, and she remains the only person honored in two different sciences, physics and chemistry.

facts.ja: グーテンベルクが活版印刷を発明した1440年代、日本は室町時代だった。
facts.easy: When Gutenberg made his printing machine in the 1440s, Japan was in the Muromachi period.
facts.std: When Gutenberg developed his printing press in the 1440s, Japan was in the Muromachi period.

facts.ja: パスポートが広く必要になったのは第一次世界大戦のころから。それ以前は、多くの国境を書類なしで越えられた。
facts.easy: Before the First World War, people could often cross borders without a passport.
facts.std: Passports became widely required only around the First World War; before that, many borders could be crossed without papers.

facts.ja: 1969年のアポロ11号の月面着陸のとき、管制室のスタッフの平均年齢は28歳ほどだったといわれる。
facts.easy: When people first walked on the moon, the team in the control room was very young, about 28 on average.
facts.std: During the Apollo 11 Moon landing in 1969, the average age of the mission control team is said to have been about 28.

facts.ja: 第一次世界大戦は「クリスマスまでに終わる」と言われていたが、4年以上続き、1500万人以上が亡くなった。
facts.easy: People said the First World War would end by Christmas. It lasted more than four years.
facts.std: Many expected the First World War to be over by Christmas, but it lasted more than four years and killed over 15 million people.

facts.ja: 縄文土器は1万5千年以上前にさかのぼり、世界でも最も古い土器のひとつ。
facts.easy: Some of the oldest pots in the world were made in Japan more than 15,000 years ago.
facts.std: Jōmon pottery from Japan dates back more than 15,000 years, making it among the oldest pottery in the world.

facts.ja: 日本は元号（令和など）を今も公式に使っている唯一の国。最初の元号「大化」は645年で、約1400年の歴史がある。
facts.easy: Japan is the only country that still uses era names, like Reiwa. The first one began in the year 645.
facts.std: Japan is the only country still officially using era names such as Reiwa. The first, Taika, began in 645, nearly 1,400 years ago.

facts.ja: アメリカ独立宣言とアダム・スミスの『国富論』は、どちらも1776年に出た。
facts.easy: The American Declaration of Independence and Adam Smith's famous book came out in the same year, 1776.
facts.std: The US Declaration of Independence and Adam Smith's The Wealth of Nations were both published in 1776.

facts.ja: ヴェルサイユ宮殿のぜいたくな建設と維持の費用は、フランスの財政を苦しめた理由のひとつと言われる。
facts.easy: Building the great palace of Versailles cost so much money that it hurt France's economy.
facts.std: The huge cost of building and running the Palace of Versailles is often cited as one strain on French finances before the Revolution.

facts.ja: 古代エジプトでは猫が大切にされ、飼い猫が死ぬと家族がまゆ毛をそって悲しみを表したと伝えられる。
facts.easy: In old Egypt, cats were very special. When a cat died, the family cut off their eyebrows to show they were sad.
facts.std: In ancient Egypt cats were highly respected; according to Herodotus, families shaved their eyebrows in mourning when a pet cat died.

facts.ja: 古代ローマでは鉛を使った水道管や容器が広く使われ、人々が鉛中毒になっていたという説がある。
facts.easy: People in old Rome used a lot of lead. Some people think this made them sick.
facts.std: Ancient Romans used lead widely in pipes and cookware, and some historians suggest lead poisoning harmed public health.

facts.ja: 眼鏡は13世紀のイタリアで発明された。
facts.easy: Glasses for the eyes were first made in Italy in the 1200s.
facts.std: Eyeglasses were invented in Italy in the late 13th century.

facts.ja: 明治維新（1868年）から1945年まではわずか77年。そのあいだに日本は急速に近代化した。
facts.easy: Japan changed very quickly in only 77 years, from 1868 to 1945.
facts.std: Only 77 years passed between the Meiji Restoration in 1868 and 1945, a period of remarkably rapid modernization for Japan.

facts.ja: 最古級の文字「楔形文字」は約5000年前のメソポタミア（今のイラク）で生まれた。最初は物の数の記録に使われた。
facts.easy: One of the first kinds of writing began about 5,000 years ago in what is now Iraq. It was first used to count goods.
facts.std: Cuneiform, one of the earliest writing systems, appeared in Mesopotamia, now Iraq, about 5,000 years ago and was first used to keep records of goods.

facts.ja: money（お金）は、ローマの女神ユノ・モネタの神殿で硬貨が作られていたことに由来する。
facts.easy: 'Money' comes from Juno Moneta, a Roman goddess. Coins were made at her temple.
facts.std: 'Money' comes from Juno Moneta, the Roman goddess at whose temple coins were minted.

facts.ja: bank（銀行）は、イタリア語の banca（長いす・台）から。両替商が台の上でお金をやりとりしていた。
facts.easy: 'Bank' comes from an Italian word for 'bench'. Money changers worked at benches.
facts.std: 'Bank' comes from Italian banca, 'bench', where early money changers did business.

facts.ja: bankrupt（破産した）は、イタリア語の banca rotta（壊れた台）から。破産した両替商の台を壊した習慣に由来すると言われる。
facts.easy: 'Bankrupt' comes from Italian words meaning 'broken bench'.
facts.std: 'Bankrupt' comes from Italian banca rotta, 'broken bench', reportedly from the practice of breaking a failed money changer's bench.

facts.ja: lord（主人）は古い英語の hlāfweard（パンの番人）から。lady は「パンをこねる人」が語源とされる。
facts.easy: 'Lord' once meant 'guardian of the bread', and 'lady' meant 'bread maker'.
facts.std: 'Lord' comes from Old English hlāfweard, 'loaf-keeper', and 'lady' from a word meaning 'loaf-kneader'.

facts.ja: clue（手がかり）は、古い英語の clew（糸の玉）から。ギリシャ神話で迷宮から出るのに糸玉を使った話にちなむ。
facts.easy: 'Clue' comes from 'clew', a ball of thread. In a Greek story, a hero used thread to find his way out of a maze.
facts.std: 'Clue' comes from 'clew', a ball of thread, recalling the Greek myth in which Theseus used thread to escape the labyrinth.

facts.ja: travel（旅行）は travail（苦労・骨折り）と同じ語源。昔の旅はとても大変だった。
facts.easy: 'Travel' comes from the same word as 'travail', meaning hard work. Old journeys were very hard.
facts.std: 'Travel' shares its origin with 'travail', 'toil', reflecting how hard journeys once were.

facts.ja: nice は、もとはラテン語の nescius（知らない）から来た言葉で、中世の英語では「愚かな」という意味だった。
facts.easy: 'Nice' once meant 'foolish'. Its meaning changed over hundreds of years.
facts.std: 'Nice' comes from Latin nescius, 'ignorant', and in Middle English meant 'foolish' before gradually shifting to 'pleasant'.

facts.ja: awful はもとは「畏れ（awe）に満ちた」という意味で、よい意味でも使われた。今は「ひどい」という悪い意味になった。
facts.easy: 'Awful' first meant 'full of awe'. Now it means 'very bad'.
facts.std: 'Awful' originally meant 'inspiring awe', sometimes in a positive sense, before coming to mean 'very bad'.

facts.ja: planet（惑星）はギリシャ語の「さまよう者」から。星座の中を動き回って見えることから。
facts.easy: 'Planet' comes from a Greek word meaning 'wanderer'. Planets seem to move among the stars.
facts.std: 'Planet' comes from Greek planētēs, 'wanderer', because planets appear to move across the fixed stars.

facts.ja: virus（ウイルス）はラテン語で「毒」という意味。
facts.easy: 'Virus' comes from a Latin word meaning 'poison'.
facts.std: 'Virus' comes from Latin virus, meaning 'poison' or 'slimy liquid'.

facts.ja: fan（熱心なファン）は、fanatic（熱狂的な人）を縮めた言葉。19世紀末のアメリカの野球で使われ始めたとされる。
facts.easy: 'Fan' is a short form of 'fanatic'. It started with baseball in the 1800s.
facts.std: 'Fan' is a shortening of 'fanatic', first used for baseball enthusiasts in late 19th-century America.

facts.ja: bus（バス）は omnibus の短縮。omnibus はラテン語で「すべての人のために」という意味。
facts.easy: 'Bus' is short for 'omnibus', which means 'for everyone' in Latin.
facts.std: 'Bus' is short for 'omnibus', Latin for 'for all', since it carried anyone who paid.

facts.ja: taxi と cab は、taximeter cabriolet（料金メーター付きの軽い馬車）の短縮から。
facts.easy: 'Taxi' and 'cab' come from 'taximeter cabriolet', a carriage with a fare meter.
facts.std: Both 'taxi' and 'cab' are shortenings of 'taximeter cabriolet', a light carriage fitted with a fare meter.

facts.ja: trivia（ささいな知識・雑学）は、ラテン語の trivium（三本の道が交わる所）から。人が集まって世間話をする場所だった。
facts.easy: 'Trivia' comes from a Latin word for a place where three roads meet. People chatted there.
facts.std: 'Trivia' comes from Latin trivium, a place where three roads meet, where people gathered for small talk.

facts.ja: photograph はギリシャ語の「光（phōs）で描く（graphē）」から。
facts.easy: 'Photograph' means 'drawing with light' in Greek.
facts.std: 'Photograph' comes from Greek words meaning 'light' and 'drawing': drawing with light.

facts.ja: telephone はギリシャ語の「遠く（tele）の声（phōnē）」から。television は「遠くを見る」。
facts.easy: 'Telephone' means 'far voice', and 'television' means 'far seeing'.
facts.std: 'Telephone' combines Greek tele, 'far', and phōnē, 'voice'; 'television' adds Latin visio, 'seeing'.

facts.ja: restaurant はフランス語の restaurer（回復させる）から。もとは体力を回復させるスープを指した。
facts.easy: 'Restaurant' comes from a French word meaning 'to restore'. It first meant a soup that gave you energy.
facts.std: 'Restaurant' comes from French restaurer, 'to restore', originally referring to a restorative broth.

facts.ja: hotel, hospital, hostel, hospitality はすべてラテン語の hospes（客・もてなす人）から来ている。
facts.easy: 'Hotel', 'hospital', and 'hostel' all come from a Latin word for 'guest' or 'host'.
facts.std: 'Hotel', 'hospital', 'hostel' and 'hospitality' all derive from Latin hospes, 'guest' or 'host'.

facts.ja: vacation（休暇）は、ラテン語の vacare（空である）から。仕事のない「空いた」時間。vacant（空いている）と同じ語源。
facts.easy: 'Vacation' comes from a Latin word meaning 'to be empty', like 'vacant'.
facts.std: 'Vacation' comes from Latin vacare, 'to be empty or free', the same root as 'vacant'.

facts.ja: compete（競争する）はラテン語の competere（一緒に求める）から。もとは「同じものを一緒に目指す」という意味。
facts.easy: 'Compete' comes from Latin words meaning 'to seek together'.
facts.std: 'Compete' comes from Latin competere, 'to strive together' or 'to seek the same thing'.

facts.ja: candidate（候補者）は、ラテン語の candidatus（白い服を着た）から。古代ローマで公職を目指す人は白いトーガを着た。
facts.easy: 'Candidate' comes from a Latin word for 'dressed in white'. Roman candidates wore white.
facts.std: 'Candidate' comes from Latin candidatus, 'clothed in white', because Roman office-seekers wore white togas.

facts.ja: calendar はラテン語の kalendae（毎月1日）から。ローマでは月の1日に借金を返す習慣があった。
facts.easy: 'Calendar' comes from the Latin word for the first day of each month.
facts.std: 'Calendar' comes from Latin kalendae, the first day of the month, when debts were traditionally due in Rome.

facts.ja: paper（紙）は、古代エジプトで使われたパピルス（papyrus）から。
facts.easy: 'Paper' comes from 'papyrus', a plant used for writing in ancient Egypt.
facts.std: 'Paper' comes from 'papyrus', the plant-based writing material of ancient Egypt.

facts.ja: Bible（聖書）は、ギリシャ語の biblion（本）から。さらにさかのぼると、パピルスの輸出で知られた港町ビブロスにたどり着く。
facts.easy: 'Bible' comes from a Greek word for 'book', named after the city of Byblos.
facts.std: 'Bible' comes from Greek biblion, 'book', ultimately from Byblos, a port famous for exporting papyrus.

facts.ja: boss（上司）はオランダ語の baas（親方）から。ニューヨークに住んだオランダ系の人々の言葉がアメリカ英語に広まった。
facts.easy: 'Boss' comes from the Dutch word 'baas', meaning master.
facts.std: 'Boss' came into American English from Dutch baas, 'master', used by early Dutch settlers in New York.

facts.ja: agenda（議題）は、ラテン語で「なされるべきことども」という意味。
facts.easy: 'Agenda' is Latin for 'things to be done'.
facts.std: 'Agenda' is Latin for 'things to be done'.

facts.ja: memo（メモ）は memorandum の短縮で、ラテン語で「覚えておくべきこと」。
facts.easy: 'Memo' is short for 'memorandum', Latin for 'something to remember'.
facts.std: 'Memo' is short for 'memorandum', Latin for 'a thing to be remembered'.

facts.ja: pen（ペン）は、ラテン語の penna（羽根）から。昔は鳥の羽根ペンで書いていた。
facts.easy: 'Pen' comes from a Latin word for 'feather'. People wrote with feathers.
facts.std: 'Pen' comes from Latin penna, 'feather', from the days of quill pens.

facts.ja: pencil（鉛筆）は、ラテン語の penicillus（小さなしっぽ＝絵筆）から。ペニシリンも同じ語源（筆のような形のカビ）。
facts.easy: 'Pencil' comes from a Latin word for a small brush. 'Penicillin' has the same root.
facts.std: 'Pencil' comes from Latin penicillus, 'little tail' or 'paintbrush'; penicillin is named from the same word because of the mold's brush-like shape.

facts.ja: alphabet は、ギリシャ文字の最初の2文字 alpha と beta をつなげた言葉。
facts.easy: 'Alphabet' comes from the first two Greek letters, alpha and beta.
facts.std: 'Alphabet' combines alpha and beta, the first two letters of the Greek alphabet.

facts.ja: education はラテン語の educare（育てる）から。「中から引き出す」という意味の educere と結びつけて説明されることも多い。
facts.easy: 'Education' comes from Latin words meaning 'to bring up' or 'to lead out'.
facts.std: 'Education' comes from Latin educare, 'to bring up', often linked with educere, 'to lead out'.

facts.ja: friend は古い英語の frēond（愛する人）から。free と同じ「愛する」という意味の語根にさかのぼる。
facts.easy: 'Friend' comes from an old English word meaning 'one who loves'.
facts.std: 'Friend' comes from Old English frēond, 'one who loves', from the same root as 'free'.

facts.ja: flower（花）と flour（小麦粉）は、もとは同じ言葉。flour は「穀物のいちばんよい部分（花）」という意味だった。
facts.easy: 'Flower' and 'flour' were once the same word. Flour was 'the best part' of grain.
facts.std: 'Flower' and 'flour' were originally the same word; flour was the 'flower', or finest part, of ground grain.

facts.ja: mind と mental、memory はインド・ヨーロッパ語の「考える」という語根にさかのぼるとされる。
facts.easy: 'Mind' and 'mental' come from very old words meaning 'to think'.
facts.std: 'Mind' and 'mental' trace back to an ancient Indo-European root meaning 'to think'.

facts.ja: economy（経済）は、ギリシャ語の oikos（家）＋ nomos（管理）から。もとは「家の切り盛り」という意味。
facts.easy: 'Economy' comes from Greek words meaning 'managing a house'.
facts.std: 'Economy' comes from Greek oikonomia, from oikos, 'house', and nomos, 'management': household management.

facts.ja: ecology（生態学）も economy と同じ oikos（家）から。自然を「生き物の家」と見る考え方。
facts.easy: 'Ecology' also comes from the Greek word for 'house'. Nature is a home for living things.
facts.std: 'Ecology' also comes from Greek oikos, 'house', treating nature as the household of living things.

facts.ja: democracy はギリシャ語の dēmos（民衆）＋ kratos（力）から。「民衆の支配」という意味。
facts.easy: 'Democracy' means 'power of the people' in Greek.
facts.std: 'Democracy' comes from Greek dēmos, 'people', and kratos, 'power' or 'rule'.

facts.ja: idiot はギリシャ語の idiōtēs（私人・公職につかない人）から。もとは悪口ではなかった。
facts.easy: 'Idiot' comes from a Greek word for a private person who did not take part in public life.
facts.std: 'Idiot' comes from Greek idiōtēs, a private citizen who did not hold public office, and was not originally an insult.

facts.ja: person はラテン語の persona（俳優の仮面）から。仮面を通して（per）声が響く（sonare）からという説がある。
facts.easy: 'Person' comes from a Latin word for an actor's mask.
facts.std: 'Person' comes from Latin persona, 'actor's mask', sometimes explained as the mask through which the voice sounded.

facts.ja: holiday（休日）は holy day（聖なる日）から。もとは宗教の祝日のこと。
facts.easy: 'Holiday' comes from 'holy day'.
facts.std: 'Holiday' comes from 'holy day', originally a religious festival.

facts.ja: month（月）は moon（月）と同じ語源。月の満ち欠けの周期がもとになっている。
facts.easy: 'Month' comes from the same word as 'moon'.
facts.std: 'Month' shares its origin with 'moon', since months were based on the lunar cycle.

facts.ja: focus はラテン語で「炉・かまど」の意味。家の中心である火のある場所から「焦点」の意味になった。
facts.easy: 'Focus' is the Latin word for 'fireplace'. The fire was the center of the home.
facts.std: 'Focus' is Latin for 'hearth', the center of the home, and came to mean a central point.

facts.ja: soldier（兵士）はラテン語の solidus（ローマの金貨）から。給料をもらって戦う人という意味。
facts.easy: 'Soldier' comes from 'solidus', a Roman gold coin. Soldiers were paid to fight.
facts.std: 'Soldier' comes from solidus, a Roman gold coin, referring to someone who fights for pay.

facts.ja: freelance（フリーランス）は、中世の雇われ騎士「free lance（自由な槍）」から。19世紀の小説で使われて広まった。
facts.easy: 'Freelance' first meant a knight who would fight for anyone who paid him.
facts.std: 'Freelance' originally described a medieval mercenary, a 'free lance', and was popularized by a 19th-century novel.

facts.ja: target（的）は、古いフランス語の targe（小さな盾）から。盾が的として使われた。
facts.easy: 'Target' comes from an old French word for a small shield.
facts.std: 'Target' comes from Old French targe, 'small shield', which was used as something to aim at.

facts.ja: astronaut は、ギリシャ語の「星（astron）の船乗り（nautēs）」から。
facts.easy: 'Astronaut' means 'star sailor' in Greek.
facts.std: 'Astronaut' comes from Greek astron, 'star', and nautēs, 'sailor'.

facts.ja: nausea（吐き気）はギリシャ語の naus（船）から。もとは船酔いのこと。navy（海軍）も同じ語源。
facts.easy: 'Nausea' comes from the Greek word for 'ship'. It first meant seasickness.
facts.std: 'Nausea' comes from Greek naus, 'ship', originally meaning seasickness; 'navy' shares the same root.

facts.ja: tax（税）と taxi は語源的につながっている。taxi の taximeter はラテン語の taxa（料金）に由来する。
facts.easy: 'Taxi' and 'tax' are related. Both come from a Latin word about charges.
facts.std: 'Tax' and 'taxi' are related: the taximeter takes its name from Medieval Latin taxa, 'charge'.

facts.ja: quarantine（隔離）は、イタリア語の quaranta giorni（40日間）から。ペストの時代、船を40日間港の外に留めた。
facts.easy: 'Quarantine' comes from Italian words meaning '40 days'. Ships waited 40 days during the plague.
facts.std: 'Quarantine' comes from Italian quaranta giorni, '40 days', the period ships were isolated during plague outbreaks.

facts.ja: rival（ライバル）はラテン語の rivalis（同じ川を使う人）から。川（rivus）の水をめぐって争ったことに由来する。
facts.easy: 'Rival' comes from a Latin word for people who use the same stream.
facts.std: 'Rival' comes from Latin rivalis, 'one using the same stream', from rivus, 'stream'.

facts.ja: 日本のお辞儀は角度で意味が変わる。軽い会釈は約15度、ていねいなお辞儀は約30度、深い謝罪や感謝は約45度と言われる。
facts.easy: In Japan, the angle of a bow matters. A small bow is about 15 degrees, and a deep bow is about 45 degrees.
facts.std: Japanese bows vary by angle: roughly 15 degrees for a casual greeting, 30 for a polite bow and 45 for deep thanks or apology.

facts.ja: アメリカのレストランでは、料金の15〜20％程度のチップを払うのが一般的。
facts.easy: In American restaurants, people usually leave a tip of about 15 to 20 percent.
facts.std: In the United States, tipping restaurant servers around 15 to 20 percent of the bill is customary.

facts.ja: 日本では一般にチップの習慣がなく、渡そうとすると断られることもある。
facts.easy: In Japan, people usually do not give tips. Staff may even refuse them.
facts.std: Tipping is generally not practiced in Japan, and staff may politely refuse a tip.

facts.ja: フランスでは、親しい人とのあいさつで頬を軽く合わせる「ビズ」をする。回数は地方によって2回から4回まで違う。
facts.easy: In France, friends greet each other with kisses on the cheeks. The number of kisses depends on the region.
facts.std: In France, friends greet each other with 'la bise', cheek kisses whose number—from two to four—varies by region.

facts.ja: ブルガリアでは、首を縦に振ると「いいえ」、横に振ると「はい」を表すことがある。
facts.easy: In Bulgaria, nodding your head can mean 'no', and shaking it can mean 'yes'.
facts.std: In Bulgaria, a nod can mean 'no' and a head shake 'yes', the reverse of most countries.

facts.ja: 親指と人さし指で輪を作る「OK」のしぐさは、国によっては失礼な意味になる。日本ではお金を表すことも多い。
facts.easy: The 'OK' hand sign can be rude in some countries. In Japan, it can also mean money.
facts.std: The circle-shaped 'OK' gesture is offensive in some countries, while in Japan it often signifies money.

facts.ja: 親指を立てる「グッド」のしぐさは、中東や西アフリカの一部などでは失礼な意味になることがある。
facts.easy: A 'thumbs up' is friendly in many places, but rude in some parts of the world.
facts.std: A thumbs-up is positive in many countries but can be offensive in parts of the Middle East and West Africa.

facts.ja: 日本では、箸から箸へ食べ物を渡す「箸渡し」は、葬儀の骨上げを思わせるので避けられる。
facts.easy: In Japan, people do not pass food from chopsticks to chopsticks. It reminds people of funerals.
facts.std: In Japan, passing food directly from one pair of chopsticks to another is avoided because it echoes a funeral ritual.

facts.ja: ご飯に箸を立てる「立て箸」は、仏壇に供えるご飯を思わせるため、日本や中国などで嫌われる。
facts.easy: In Japan and China, you should not stand chopsticks up in rice. It looks like an offering for the dead.
facts.std: Standing chopsticks upright in rice is taboo in Japan, China and elsewhere because it resembles offerings to the dead.

facts.ja: 日本では麺をすすって音を立てて食べてもよいとされるが、欧米では多くの場合マナー違反とされる。
facts.easy: In Japan, it is OK to slurp noodles. In many Western countries, it is seen as rude.
facts.std: Slurping noodles is acceptable in Japan, but in many Western countries eating noisily is considered impolite.

facts.ja: インドや中東などでは、食事やものの受け渡しに右手を使うのが基本。左手は不浄とされることがある。
facts.easy: In India and the Middle East, people usually eat and give things with the right hand.
facts.std: In India and much of the Middle East, the right hand is used for eating and handing things over, as the left is traditionally seen as unclean.

facts.ja: 中国では、時計を贈るのは縁起が悪いとされる。「時計を送る（送钟）」が「最期をみとる（送终）」と同じ発音だから。
facts.easy: In China, a clock is a bad gift. The words for 'giving a clock' sound like 'attending a death'.
facts.std: In China, giving a clock is considered unlucky because 'giving a clock' sounds like a phrase for attending someone's death.

facts.ja: 日本・中国・韓国では、4は「死」と同じ発音のため縁起が悪いとされ、4階や4号室がないビルもある。
facts.easy: In Japan, China, and Korea, 4 is unlucky because it sounds like 'death'. Some buildings have no 4th floor.
facts.std: In Japan, China and Korea, four is considered unlucky because it sounds like 'death', so some buildings skip the fourth floor.

facts.ja: 欧米では13が不吉な数とされ、13階を飛ばすビルやホテルがある。
facts.easy: In many Western countries, 13 is unlucky. Some hotels have no 13th floor.
facts.std: In many Western countries 13 is considered unlucky, and some buildings skip the 13th floor.

facts.ja: 中国では8は「発（栄える）」と発音が似ているため縁起のよい数。北京オリンピックは2008年8月8日午後8時8分に開幕した。
facts.easy: In China, 8 is a lucky number. The Beijing Olympics started on 8/8/2008 at 8:08 pm.
facts.std: Eight is lucky in China because it sounds like the word for prosperity; the Beijing Olympics opened at 8:08 pm on 8 August 2008.

facts.ja: 中国の旧正月（春節）には、赤い封筒（紅包）にお金を入れて子どもなどに渡す。赤は幸運の色とされる。
facts.easy: At Chinese New Year, people give money in red envelopes. Red is a lucky color.
facts.std: During Chinese New Year, money is given in red envelopes, as red symbolizes good luck.

facts.ja: ロシアなどでは、お祝いの花束は奇数本で贈る。偶数本はお葬式の花とされる。
facts.easy: In Russia, people give an odd number of flowers. Even numbers are for funerals.
facts.std: In Russia and some nearby countries, bouquets for happy occasions have an odd number of flowers, as even numbers are for funerals.

facts.ja: 菊の花は日本では皇室の紋章として大切にされる一方、フランスやイタリアなどでは主にお墓に供える花とされる。
facts.easy: In Japan, the chrysanthemum is a royal symbol. In France and Italy, it is a flower for graves.
facts.std: The chrysanthemum is an imperial emblem in Japan, but in France and Italy it is mainly associated with graves and funerals.

facts.ja: 誕生日にろうそくを立ててケーキを食べる習慣は、18世紀のドイツの子どもの誕生日祝いにさかのぼるとされる。
facts.easy: Birthday cakes with candles go back to children's parties in Germany in the 1700s.
facts.std: Birthday cakes with candles trace back to 18th-century German children's birthday celebrations called Kinderfeste.

facts.ja: 中国では誕生日に「長寿麺」を食べる習慣がある。長い麺は長生きの象徴で、切らずに食べるのがよいとされる。
facts.easy: In China, people eat long noodles on birthdays. Long noodles mean a long life.
facts.std: In China, people eat 'longevity noodles' on birthdays; the long, uncut noodles symbolize a long life.

facts.ja: スペインでは大みそかの夜、時計の鐘に合わせて12粒のブドウを食べると、新しい年の幸運を呼ぶとされる。
facts.easy: In Spain, people eat 12 grapes at midnight on New Year's Eve for good luck.
facts.std: In Spain, people eat twelve grapes at midnight on New Year's Eve, one for each chime of the clock, for luck in each month.

facts.ja: 日本の大みそかの除夜の鐘は108回つく。人間の煩悩の数とされる。
facts.easy: In Japan, temple bells ring 108 times on New Year's Eve.
facts.std: On New Year's Eve, Japanese temples ring their bells 108 times, a number associated with human desires in Buddhism.

facts.ja: 日本でクリスマスにフライドチキンを食べる習慣は、1974年ごろに始まったKFCの広告がきっかけで広まった。
facts.easy: Many Japanese families eat fried chicken at Christmas. This started with KFC ads in the 1970s.
facts.std: Eating fried chicken at Christmas in Japan became popular after a KFC marketing campaign that began around 1974.

facts.ja: 日本ではバレンタインデーに女性が男性にチョコレートを贈り、3月14日のホワイトデーにお返しをする習慣がある。
facts.easy: In Japan, women give chocolate on Valentine's Day. Men give gifts back on White Day, March 14.
facts.std: In Japan, women traditionally give chocolate on Valentine's Day, and men reciprocate on White Day, March 14.

facts.ja: アメリカの感謝祭（サンクスギビング）は11月の第4木曜日。七面鳥を食べる家庭が多い。
facts.easy: Thanksgiving in the US is on the fourth Thursday of November. Many families eat turkey.
facts.std: American Thanksgiving falls on the fourth Thursday of November, and many families eat roast turkey.

facts.ja: カナダの感謝祭は10月の第2月曜日で、アメリカより約1か月半早い。
facts.easy: Canada's Thanksgiving is on the second Monday of October.
facts.std: Canadian Thanksgiving is celebrated on the second Monday of October, about six weeks before the American holiday.

facts.ja: ハロウィンのかぼちゃのランタンは、もとはアイルランドなどでカブで作られていた。アメリカに伝わり、かぼちゃになった。
facts.easy: Halloween lanterns were first made from turnips in Ireland. In America, people used pumpkins.
facts.std: Jack-o'-lanterns were originally carved from turnips in Ireland and Scotland; immigrants to America switched to pumpkins.

facts.ja: メキシコの「死者の日」（11月1〜2日）は、亡くなった家族を明るく迎える祭り。カラフルなガイコツの飾りが有名。
facts.easy: Mexico's Day of the Dead is a happy festival to remember family who have died.
facts.std: Mexico's Day of the Dead, on November 1 and 2, cheerfully welcomes the spirits of departed relatives, with colorful skull decorations.

facts.ja: 日本のお盆は、先祖の霊が家に帰ってくるとされる夏の行事。迎え火や送り火をたく地域がある。
facts.easy: Obon is a summer event in Japan. People believe their ancestors' spirits come home.
facts.std: Obon is a Japanese summer observance when ancestral spirits are believed to return home, welcomed and sent off with fires in some regions.

facts.ja: インドのホーリー祭では、春の訪れを祝って色の粉や水をかけ合う。
facts.easy: During the Holi festival in India, people throw colored powder at each other to welcome spring.
facts.std: During Holi, India's festival of spring, people celebrate by throwing colored powder and water at each other.

facts.ja: インドのディワリ（光の祭り）では、家々に灯りをともして悪に対する善の勝利を祝う。
facts.easy: Diwali is the festival of lights in India. People light lamps in their homes.
facts.std: Diwali, the Hindu festival of lights, celebrates the victory of light over darkness with lamps lit in homes.

facts.ja: イスラム教のラマダン月には、多くの人が日の出から日没まで飲食をしない。ビジネスの予定にも影響することがある。
facts.easy: During Ramadan, many Muslims do not eat or drink from sunrise to sunset.
facts.std: During the month of Ramadan, many Muslims fast from dawn to sunset, which can affect business hours and meeting schedules.

facts.ja: イスラム圏の多くの国では、週末は金曜日と土曜日。金曜日は集団礼拝の日である。
facts.easy: In many Muslim countries, the weekend is Friday and Saturday.
facts.std: In many Muslim-majority countries the weekend falls on Friday and Saturday, since Friday is the day of congregational prayer.

facts.ja: アラブ首長国連邦は2022年から、公的機関の週末を土日（金曜は半日勤務）に変えた。世界の市場と合わせるためだった。
facts.easy: In 2022, the UAE moved its weekend to Saturday and Sunday to match world markets.
facts.std: In 2022, the United Arab Emirates moved its official weekend to Saturday and Sunday, with a half day on Friday, to align with global markets.

facts.ja: スペインでは昼食後に休憩する「シエスタ」の習慣があり、昼過ぎに閉まる店もある。ただし都市部では減っている。
facts.easy: In Spain, some shops close in the afternoon for a rest called 'siesta'.
facts.std: In Spain, the tradition of the siesta means some shops close in the early afternoon, though the custom is fading in big cities.

facts.ja: スペインでは夕食の時間が遅く、午後9時〜10時ごろに食べるのも普通。
facts.easy: In Spain, people often eat dinner at 9 or 10 pm.
facts.std: Spaniards typically eat dinner late, often around 9 or 10 in the evening.

facts.ja: スウェーデンには「フィーカ」という習慣があり、職場でも仲間とコーヒーと甘いものを楽しむ休憩をとる。
facts.easy: In Sweden, 'fika' is a coffee break with friends or coworkers, often with something sweet.
facts.std: 'Fika' is a Swedish custom of taking a coffee break with colleagues or friends, usually with a pastry.

facts.ja: イギリスでは、午後に紅茶と軽食を楽しむ「アフタヌーンティー」の習慣が19世紀に広まった。
facts.easy: In Britain, 'afternoon tea' with small cakes became popular in the 1800s.
facts.std: Afternoon tea, with sandwiches and cakes, became fashionable in Britain in the 1840s.

facts.ja: モロッコなどでは、客にミントティーをふるまうのがもてなしの基本。高い位置から注いで泡を立てる。
facts.easy: In Morocco, people welcome guests with mint tea. They pour it from high up.
facts.std: In Morocco, serving sweet mint tea, poured from a height to create foam, is a central part of hospitality.

facts.ja: アルゼンチンなどでは、マテ茶を一つの容器と金属のストローで回し飲みする習慣がある。
facts.easy: In Argentina, friends share mate tea from one cup with one metal straw.
facts.std: In Argentina, Uruguay and nearby countries, friends share mate from a single gourd with a metal straw, passing it around the group.

facts.ja: イギリスのパブでは、仲間の分も順番に注文して払う「ラウンド」という習慣がある。
facts.easy: In British pubs, friends take turns buying drinks for the whole group. This is called a 'round'.
facts.std: In British pubs, friends often take turns buying drinks for the whole group, a custom known as 'buying a round'.

facts.ja: 日本や韓国では、お酒の席で自分のグラスに自分で注がず、互いに注ぎ合うのがマナーとされることが多い。
facts.easy: In Japan and Korea, people often pour drinks for each other, not for themselves.
facts.std: In Japan and Korea, it is customary at drinking gatherings to pour for others rather than for yourself.

facts.ja: 韓国では目上の人とお酒を飲むとき、顔を少し横に向けて飲むのが礼儀とされる。
facts.easy: In Korea, when drinking with an older person, people turn their face a little to the side.
facts.std: In Korea, when drinking with an elder or superior, it is polite to turn your head slightly away as you drink.

facts.ja: ドイツなどでは乾杯のとき、相手の目を見るのがマナー。目をそらすと縁起が悪いという言い伝えもある。
facts.easy: In Germany, people look each other in the eye when they say 'cheers'.
facts.std: In Germany, making eye contact while clinking glasses is expected; a popular superstition says not doing so brings bad luck.

facts.ja: フランスの食事は、前菜・メイン・チーズ・デザートと順番に出るのが一般的。チーズはデザートの前に食べる。
facts.easy: In France, cheese is often served after the main dish and before dessert.
facts.std: In a traditional French meal, the cheese course comes after the main dish and before dessert.

facts.ja: イタリアでは、食後に牛乳たっぷりのカプチーノを飲むことはあまりない。カプチーノは主に朝の飲み物とされる。
facts.easy: In Italy, cappuccino is mostly a morning drink. People rarely drink it after dinner.
facts.std: In Italy, cappuccino is mainly a breakfast drink, and ordering one after a meal is unusual.

facts.ja: イタリアのパスタは、多くの場合メインの肉料理の前に食べる「第一の皿（プリモ・ピアット）」。
facts.easy: In Italy, pasta is often a first course, before the meat dish.
facts.std: In a traditional Italian meal, pasta is usually the primo, or first course, served before the main meat or fish dish.

facts.ja: エチオピアでは、インジェラという薄いパンで料理を包み、手で食べる。大皿を皆で囲むのが一般的。
facts.easy: In Ethiopia, people eat with their hands using a flat bread called injera. They share one big plate.
facts.std: In Ethiopia, meals are eaten by hand from a shared platter, using injera, a spongy flatbread, to scoop up food.

facts.ja: アメリカでは、ナイフで切った後にフォークを右手に持ちかえて食べる人が多い。ヨーロッパでは左手にフォークを持ったまま食べるのが一般的。
facts.easy: Many Americans cut food, then move the fork to the right hand. Europeans usually keep the fork in the left hand.
facts.std: Many Americans cut food and then switch the fork to the right hand to eat, while Europeans typically keep the fork in the left.

facts.ja: 中国の宴席では、料理を少し残すことが「十分にもてなしてもらった」という意味になることがある。
facts.easy: At a Chinese dinner, leaving a little food can show that the host gave you enough.
facts.std: At Chinese banquets, leaving a little food on the plate can signal that the host has provided more than enough.

facts.ja: 日本や韓国、北欧などでは、家に入るときに靴を脱ぐ習慣がある。
facts.easy: In Japan, Korea, and Nordic countries, people take off their shoes at home.
facts.std: Removing shoes before entering a home is customary in Japan, Korea and much of Scandinavia, among other places.

facts.ja: フィンランドにはサウナが約300万あると言われ、人口（約550万人）とほぼ同じくらい多い。
facts.easy: Finland has about 3 million saunas for about 5.5 million people.
facts.std: Finland is estimated to have around three million saunas for a population of about 5.5 million.

facts.ja: 日本の温泉や銭湯では、湯船に入る前に体を洗い、タオルを湯につけないのがマナー。
facts.easy: At Japanese hot springs, you wash your body before getting in. Do not put your towel in the water.
facts.std: At Japanese hot springs and public baths, you wash before entering the bath and keep your towel out of the water.

facts.ja: エスカレーターで立つ側は、東京ではおおむね左、大阪ではおおむね右。
facts.easy: On escalators, people stand on the left in Tokyo but on the right in Osaka.
facts.std: On escalators, people traditionally stand on the left in Tokyo but on the right in Osaka.

facts.ja: 世界の国と地域の約3分の1が車の左側通行。日本、イギリス、インド、オーストラリアなどがそう。
facts.easy: About one-third of countries drive on the left, like Japan, the UK, and India.
facts.std: About a third of the world's countries and territories drive on the left, including Japan, the UK, India and Australia.

facts.ja: スウェーデンは1967年9月3日の朝、国全体で左側通行から右側通行に切り替えた。
facts.easy: On one day in 1967, all of Sweden changed from driving on the left to driving on the right.
facts.std: On 3 September 1967, Sweden switched nationwide from driving on the left to the right, a day known as Dagen H.

facts.ja: 世界の多くの国は日付を「日・月・年」、アメリカは「月・日・年」、日本や中国は「年・月・日」の順で書く。
facts.easy: The date order is different by country. Americans write month first, and Japanese write the year first.
facts.std: Many countries write dates day-month-year, the US uses month-day-year, and Japan and China use year-month-day.

facts.ja: ドイツやフランスなどでは、小数点にコンマ、桁の区切りに点を使う。「1.000,5」は千と0.5の意味。
facts.easy: In Germany and France, people write a comma for the decimal point. '1.000,5' means one thousand and a half.
facts.std: In much of Europe, a comma marks the decimal point and periods or spaces separate thousands, so '1.000,5' means one thousand and a half.

facts.ja: アメリカでは気温を華氏で表すことが多い。華氏68度は摂氏20度。
facts.easy: In the US, temperatures are often in Fahrenheit. 68°F is 20°C.
facts.std: The United States commonly uses Fahrenheit; 68°F equals 20°C.

facts.ja: メートル法を公式に採用していない国は、アメリカ、リベリア、ミャンマーのわずか3か国とよく言われる。
facts.easy: Only three countries, including the US, do not officially use the metric system.
facts.std: The United States, Liberia and Myanmar are often cited as the only countries that have not fully adopted the metric system officially.

facts.ja: イギリスでは地上階を ground floor と呼び、その上が first floor。アメリカでは地上階が first floor。
facts.easy: In Britain, the floor at street level is the 'ground floor'. In the US, it is the 'first floor'.
facts.std: In British English the street-level floor is the 'ground floor' and the next one up is the 'first floor'; in American English, street level is the first floor.

facts.ja: アメリカや日本のカレンダーは日曜始まりが多いが、ヨーロッパの多くの国では月曜始まりが一般的。
facts.easy: Calendars in the US and Japan often start on Sunday. In much of Europe, they start on Monday.
facts.std: Calendars in the US and Japan often begin the week on Sunday, while in much of Europe Monday is the first day.

facts.ja: ドイツやスイスでは時間を守ることがとても重視され、ビジネスの約束に遅れるのは大きな失礼とされる。
facts.easy: In Germany and Switzerland, being on time is very important in business.
facts.std: In Germany and Switzerland, punctuality is highly valued, and being late for a business meeting is a serious breach of etiquette.

facts.ja: ブラジルなど中南米の一部では、パーティーに招かれたら時間ちょうどより少し遅れて着くのが普通とされる。
facts.easy: In parts of Latin America, it is normal to arrive at a party a little late.
facts.std: In parts of Latin America, such as Brazil, arriving somewhat after the stated time for a party is considered normal.

facts.ja: 中国や韓国でも、名刺は両手で渡し、両手で受け取るのが礼儀とされる。
facts.easy: In China and Korea, too, people give and receive business cards with both hands.
facts.std: In China and Korea, as in Japan, business cards are offered and received with both hands.

facts.ja: アメリカのビジネスでは、しっかりと握手し、相手の目を見ることが自信と誠実さの表れとされる。
facts.easy: In American business, a firm handshake and eye contact show confidence.
facts.std: In American business culture, a firm handshake with eye contact is seen as a sign of confidence and sincerity.

facts.ja: アメリカの職場では、上司でもファーストネームで呼び合うことが多い。
facts.easy: In American offices, people often call even their boss by first name.
facts.std: In many American workplaces, employees address even senior managers by their first names.

facts.ja: ドイツでは、博士号を持つ人を「ドクター」の肩書きつきで呼ぶことが、ビジネスでも重視されることがある。
facts.easy: In Germany, people with a doctorate are often called 'Doctor' at work.
facts.std: In Germany, academic titles such as 'Doktor' are often used in business and formal address.

facts.ja: 韓国では、相手を名前でなく「部長」「課長」など役職名で呼ぶのが一般的。
facts.easy: In Korea, people often call coworkers by their job title, like 'manager', not by name.
facts.std: In Korea, colleagues are commonly addressed by job title rather than by name.

facts.ja: アイスランドでは名字ではなく、父（または母）の名前に「〜の息子」「〜の娘」をつけた名前を使う。電話帳も名前の順に並ぶ。
facts.easy: In Iceland, people's last names come from their father's or mother's first name.
facts.std: Most Icelanders use patronymics or matronymics rather than family names, and even the phone directory is sorted by first name.

facts.ja: スペイン語圏では、父方と母方の両方の名字を持つことが多い。
facts.easy: In Spanish-speaking countries, people often have two last names: one from each parent.
facts.std: In Spanish-speaking countries, people commonly carry two surnames, one from each parent.

facts.ja: 中国や韓国では、結婚しても女性の名字が変わらないのが一般的。
facts.easy: In China and Korea, women usually keep their family name after marriage.
facts.std: In China and Korea, women traditionally keep their own family names after marriage.

facts.ja: 韓国では、金（キム）、李（イ）、朴（パク）の3つの名字で人口の4割以上を占める。
facts.easy: In Korea, more than 40% of people have one of three family names: Kim, Lee, or Park.
facts.std: In South Korea, the surnames Kim, Lee and Park together account for over 40 percent of the population.

facts.ja: 韓国では2023年から、法律上の年齢を「満年齢」に統一した。それまでは生まれた時点で1歳と数える数え方も広く使われていた。
facts.easy: Since 2023, Korea uses international age in law. Before, many people counted a baby as one year old at birth.
facts.std: In 2023, South Korea standardized on international age for legal purposes; traditionally, a baby was counted as one year old at birth.

facts.ja: 中南米の多くの国では、女の子の15歳の誕生日を「キンセアニェーラ」として盛大に祝う。
facts.easy: In many Latin American countries, a girl's 15th birthday is a big party called a quinceañera.
facts.std: Across much of Latin America, a girl's fifteenth birthday is celebrated with a large party called a quinceañera.

facts.ja: 日本の七五三は、3歳・5歳・7歳の子どもの成長を祝って神社にお参りする行事。
facts.easy: In Japan, children aged 3, 5, and 7 visit shrines to celebrate growing up. This is Shichi-Go-San.
facts.std: Shichi-Go-San is a Japanese rite in which children aged three, five and seven visit shrines to celebrate their growth.

facts.ja: 日本の成人の日は1月の第2月曜日。成人年齢は2022年に20歳から18歳に引き下げられた。
facts.easy: Japan's Coming of Age Day is in January. Since 2022, adults are 18 years old by law.
facts.std: Japan's Coming of Age Day is the second Monday of January; the legal age of adulthood was lowered from 20 to 18 in 2022.

facts.ja: 結婚指輪を左手の薬指にはめるのは、そこから心臓に直接つながる血管があるという古代ローマの言い伝えにちなむとされる。
facts.easy: People wear wedding rings on the left ring finger. An old story says a vein goes from there to the heart.
facts.std: Wearing a wedding ring on the left ring finger is linked to an ancient belief that a vein ran directly from that finger to the heart.

facts.ja: ドイツやロシア、インドなどでは、結婚指輪を右手にはめることが多い。
facts.easy: In Germany, Russia, and India, many people wear wedding rings on the right hand.
facts.std: In countries such as Germany, Russia and India, wedding rings are commonly worn on the right hand.

facts.ja: 白いウェディングドレスが広まったのは、1840年にヴィクトリア女王が白いドレスで結婚式を挙げてから。
facts.easy: White wedding dresses became popular after Queen Victoria wore one in 1840.
facts.std: White wedding dresses became fashionable after Queen Victoria wore one at her wedding in 1840.

facts.ja: 日本のご祝儀では、割り切れない奇数の金額（3万円など）がよいとされる。「縁が切れない」ようにという意味がある。
facts.easy: In Japan, wedding gift money is often an odd number, like 30,000 yen, so the couple 'cannot be split'.
facts.std: Japanese wedding gift money is traditionally an odd amount, such as 30,000 yen, because odd numbers cannot be divided evenly, symbolizing a lasting bond.

facts.ja: 日本の「お年玉」は、もとはお正月に神様に供えたお餅を分け与えたことが始まりとされる。
facts.easy: Japanese New Year money for children, 'otoshidama', started as sharing rice cakes offered to the gods.
facts.std: Japan's otoshidama, New Year money for children, is said to have originated as rice cakes offered to the gods and then shared.

facts.ja: 日本の年賀状は、元日に届くよう郵便局が年末に特別に受け付け、まとめて配達する。
facts.easy: In Japan, New Year cards are delivered on January 1 if you post them by late December.
facts.std: Japan Post holds New Year's cards posted by late December and delivers them all on January 1.

facts.ja: 英語のビジネスメールの締めには、Best regards、Kind regards、Sincerely などがよく使われる。
facts.easy: English business emails often end with 'Best regards' or 'Kind regards'.
facts.std: Common closings for English business emails include 'Best regards', 'Kind regards' and, more formally, 'Sincerely'.

facts.ja: タイでは、あいさつで両手を胸の前で合わせる「ワイ」をする。手の高さで相手への敬意の深さが変わる。
facts.easy: In Thailand, people greet each other by putting their hands together. This is called a 'wai'.
facts.std: In Thailand, the 'wai' greeting is made by pressing the palms together; the higher the hands, the greater the respect.

facts.ja: インドやネパールでは、両手を合わせて「ナマステ」とあいさつする。
facts.easy: In India and Nepal, people say 'Namaste' with their hands together.
facts.std: In India and Nepal, people greet each other with 'Namaste', pressing their palms together.

facts.ja: ニュージーランドのマオリの人々は、鼻と額を合わせる「ホンギ」というあいさつをする。
facts.easy: Māori people in New Zealand greet each other by touching noses and foreheads. This is a 'hongi'.
facts.std: The Māori of New Zealand greet with the hongi, pressing noses and foreheads together.

facts.ja: 南半球のオーストラリアでは、クリスマスは夏。浜辺やバーベキューで祝う人も多い。
facts.easy: In Australia, Christmas is in summer. Many people go to the beach or have a barbecue.
facts.std: In Australia, Christmas falls in summer, and many people celebrate at the beach or with a barbecue.

facts.ja: 日本やアジアの多くの国では、手のひらを下に向けて手招きすると「こっちへおいで」の意味。欧米の人には「あっちへ行け」に見えることがある。
facts.easy: In Japan and many Asian countries, waving with your palm down means 'come here'.
facts.std: In Japan and much of Asia, a downward-palm waving motion means 'come here', a gesture that may look like 'go away' to Westerners.

facts.ja: イタリア人は話すときに手のしぐさをよく使う。指先を上に向けてすぼめるしぐさは「何が言いたいの？」という意味。
facts.easy: Italians use many hand gestures. Fingers pinched together and pointing up can mean 'What do you mean?'
facts.std: Italians are known for expressive gestures; fingertips pinched together and pointing up often means 'What do you want?' or 'What are you saying?'

facts.ja: フィンランドでは沈黙は気まずいものではなく、言葉を選んで話す誠実さの表れと考えられることが多い。
facts.easy: In Finland, silence in a conversation is not awkward. It is often seen as respectful.
facts.std: In Finnish culture, silence in conversation is often comfortable rather than awkward, reflecting a preference for meaningful speech.

facts.ja: 文化人類学者エドワード・ホールは、言葉以外の文脈で多くを伝える文化を「高コンテクスト」、言葉ではっきり伝える文化を「低コンテクスト」と呼んだ。
facts.easy: In 'high-context' cultures, much meaning is not said. In 'low-context' cultures, people say things clearly.
facts.std: Anthropologist Edward T. Hall distinguished high-context cultures, where much meaning is implicit, from low-context cultures, where it is stated explicitly.

facts.ja: オランダには、窓のカーテンを開けたままにして家の中が見える家が多い。隠すものがないという考え方の表れとも言われる。
facts.easy: In the Netherlands, many homes leave their curtains open, so you can see inside.
facts.std: In the Netherlands, many homes leave curtains open so the interior is visible, sometimes explained as a sign of having nothing to hide.

facts.ja: オランダは人口より自転車の数が多い国として知られる。
facts.easy: The Netherlands has more bicycles than people.
facts.std: The Netherlands is known for having more bicycles than inhabitants.

facts.ja: デンマークの「ヒュッゲ」は、家族や友人とくつろいで過ごす居心地のよい時間を表す言葉。
facts.easy: 'Hygge' is a Danish word for a cozy, happy time with family or friends.
facts.std: 'Hygge' is a Danish concept of cozy, contented time spent with friends and family.

facts.ja: イギリスの郵便ポストや電話ボックスの赤色は、目立つように選ばれた色で、国の象徴になっている。
facts.easy: Red post boxes and phone boxes are famous symbols of Britain.
facts.std: Britain's red post boxes and telephone boxes were painted red to be easily seen and have become national symbols.

facts.ja: アメリカなどの英語圏では、人と話すときの心地よい距離は約45cm〜1.2m（個人的距離）と言われる。
facts.easy: In America, people usually stand about an arm's length apart when talking.
facts.std: In the United States, a comfortable distance for personal conversation is roughly 45 centimeters to 1.2 meters, according to Hall's proxemics.

facts.ja: アメリカの「How are you?」は、くわしい答えを求める質問ではなく、あいさつの一部として使われることが多い。
facts.easy: In America, 'How are you?' is often just a greeting. A short answer like 'Good, thanks' is fine.
facts.std: In the US, 'How are you?' usually functions as a greeting rather than a real question, and a short reply like 'Good, thanks' is expected.

facts.ja: 日本の「いただきます」に当たる決まった表現は英語にはない。英語圏では食事前に何も言わない人も多い。
facts.easy: English has no common phrase like 'itadakimasu'. Many people say nothing before eating.
facts.std: English has no everyday equivalent of Japanese 'itadakimasu'; many English speakers say nothing before a meal, though some say grace.

facts.ja: 英語圏では、誰かがくしゃみをすると「Bless you」と声をかけるのが一般的。ドイツ語では「Gesundheit（健康を）」と言う。
facts.easy: In English, when someone sneezes, people say 'Bless you'. In German, they say 'Gesundheit'.
facts.std: English speakers say 'Bless you' when someone sneezes, while Germans say 'Gesundheit', meaning 'health'.

facts.ja: 水星は太陽にいちばん近い惑星。大気がほとんどないため、昼は約430℃、夜は約−180℃まで温度が変わる。
facts.easy: Mercury is the closest planet to the sun. It is about 430°C in the day and −180°C at night.
facts.std: Mercury, the planet closest to the Sun, has almost no atmosphere, so temperatures swing from about 430°C by day to −180°C at night.

facts.ja: 金星は太陽系でいちばん熱い惑星。厚い二酸化炭素の大気が熱を閉じ込め、表面は約460℃にもなる。
facts.easy: Venus is the hottest planet. Its thick air traps heat, and the ground is about 460°C.
facts.std: Venus is the hottest planet in the solar system; its thick carbon dioxide atmosphere traps heat, keeping the surface around 460°C.

facts.ja: 火星には太陽系最大の火山オリンポス山がある。高さは約22kmで、エベレストの2倍以上。
facts.easy: Mars has the biggest volcano in the solar system. It is about 22 km high.
facts.std: Mars is home to Olympus Mons, the largest volcano in the solar system, about 22 kilometers high—more than twice the height of Everest.

facts.ja: 木星の1日（自転の周期）は約10時間で、太陽系の惑星の中でいちばん短い。
facts.easy: A day on Jupiter is only about 10 hours long, the shortest of all the planets.
facts.std: Jupiter spins faster than any other planet, completing one rotation in about 10 hours.

facts.ja: 土星の環の大部分は氷のかけらでできている。直径は数十万kmに広がるのに、厚さはとても薄い。
facts.easy: Saturn's rings are mostly made of pieces of ice. They are very wide but very thin.
facts.std: Saturn's rings are made mostly of chunks of water ice; they span hundreds of thousands of kilometers yet are extremely thin.

facts.ja: 人の体はおよそ37兆個の細胞でできているという推定がある（2013年の研究）。
facts.easy: One study says the human body has about 37 trillion cells.
facts.std: A 2013 study estimated that the human body contains about 37 trillion cells.

facts.ja: 人は1分間に15〜20回ほどまばたきをする。集中して画面を見ていると回数が減り、目が乾きやすくなる。
facts.easy: People blink about 15 to 20 times a minute. We blink less when we look at screens.
facts.std: People blink around 15 to 20 times a minute, but blink less while concentrating on screens, which can dry the eyes.

facts.ja: 髪の毛は1か月に約1〜1.5cm伸びる。
facts.easy: Hair grows about 1 to 1.5 centimeters a month.
facts.std: Scalp hair grows roughly one to one and a half centimeters per month.

facts.ja: 大人の体の血液は約5リットルで、体重のおよそ7〜8％にあたる。
facts.easy: An adult has about 5 liters of blood.
facts.std: An adult has about five liters of blood, roughly 7 to 8 percent of body weight.

facts.ja: 大人は1日に約2万回呼吸している。
facts.easy: Adults breathe about 20,000 times a day.
facts.std: An adult breathes roughly 20,000 times a day at rest.

facts.ja: 古代オリンピックは紀元前776年にギリシャのオリンピアで始まったと伝えられる。最初の競技は短距離走だけだった。
facts.easy: The ancient Olympic Games began in Greece in 776 BC. The first event was a short running race.
facts.std: The ancient Olympic Games are traditionally dated to 776 BC at Olympia, Greece, and at first featured only a short foot race.

facts.ja: 近代オリンピックは、フランスのクーベルタンの呼びかけで1896年にアテネで始まった。
facts.easy: The modern Olympics started in Athens in 1896, thanks to a Frenchman named Coubertin.
facts.std: The modern Olympic Games began in Athens in 1896, inspired by the French educator Pierre de Coubertin.

facts.ja: 五輪のマークの5つの輪は、5つの大陸のつながりを表す。白地と5色で、当時の世界の国旗の色がすべて描けるとされた。
facts.easy: The five Olympic rings stand for five continents joined together.
facts.std: The five Olympic rings represent the union of five continents; together with the white background, their colors were said to appear in every national flag of the time.

facts.ja: 聖火リレーが始まったのは1936年のベルリン大会から。
facts.easy: The Olympic torch relay started at the 1936 Berlin Games.
facts.std: The Olympic torch relay was first held for the 1936 Berlin Games.

facts.ja: 1964年の東京オリンピックはアジアで初めての大会。開会に合わせて東海道新幹線が開業した。
facts.easy: The 1964 Tokyo Olympics were the first in Asia. The bullet train started just before them.
facts.std: The 1964 Tokyo Olympics were the first held in Asia, and the Tokaido Shinkansen opened just in time for the Games.

facts.ja: コーヒーの木の原産地はエチオピア。ヤギがコーヒーの実を食べて元気になったのを見て発見されたという伝説がある。
facts.easy: Coffee plants come from Ethiopia. A story says goats ate the berries and became very lively.
facts.std: Coffee originated in Ethiopia; legend says a goatherd discovered it after noticing his goats became energetic after eating the berries.

facts.ja: 15世紀ごろ、イエメンでコーヒーが飲まれるようになった。積み出し港の名前「モカ」は今もコーヒーの名前に残る。
facts.easy: People in Yemen drank coffee in the 1400s. The port of Mocha gave its name to a kind of coffee.
facts.std: By the 15th century coffee was being drunk in Yemen; the port of Mocha, which shipped it, still lends its name to coffee drinks.

facts.ja: 17世紀のロンドンのコーヒーハウスは、1杯の値段で議論や情報交換ができたため「ペニー大学」と呼ばれた。
facts.easy: In the 1600s, London coffee houses were called 'penny universities'. For one penny, you could learn and talk.
facts.std: Seventeenth-century London coffeehouses were nicknamed 'penny universities' because the price of a coffee bought access to news and debate.

facts.ja: 日本には江戸時代に長崎の出島を通じてコーヒーが伝わった。本格的に広まったのは明治以降。
facts.easy: Coffee came to Japan through Nagasaki in the Edo period. It became popular after 1868.
facts.std: Coffee reached Japan through the Dutch trading post at Dejima in Nagasaki during the Edo period, but spread widely only after the Meiji era began.

facts.ja: 缶コーヒーは1969年に日本で発売されたものが世界で最初期の一つとされる。
facts.easy: Canned coffee was first sold in Japan in 1969.
facts.std: Canned coffee was popularized in Japan, with one of the earliest products launched in 1969.

facts.ja: 知られている最古の文字の一つは、約5000年前のメソポタミアの楔形文字。粘土板に葦のペンで刻んだ。
facts.easy: One of the oldest kinds of writing is cuneiform, from about 5,000 years ago. People pressed it into clay.
facts.std: Cuneiform, pressed into clay tablets with a reed stylus in Mesopotamia about 5,000 years ago, is among the oldest known writing systems.

facts.ja: 古代エジプトのヒエログリフ（聖刻文字）は、1822年にシャンポリオンがロゼッタ・ストーンなどを手がかりに解読した。
facts.easy: Egyptian hieroglyphs were understood again in 1822, with help from the Rosetta Stone.
facts.std: Egyptian hieroglyphs were deciphered by Jean-François Champollion in 1822, using the Rosetta Stone among other sources.

facts.ja: 地中海の商人だったフェニキア人の文字は、子音だけを表す22文字のアルファベット。多くの文字の祖先になった。
facts.easy: The Phoenicians were traders. Their alphabet of 22 letters became the parent of many alphabets.
facts.std: The Phoenician alphabet, 22 letters representing consonants, spread with Mediterranean traders and became the ancestor of many scripts.

facts.ja: ギリシャ人はフェニキア文字を取り入れ、母音を表す文字を加えた。母音と子音を両方書く最初のアルファベットとされる。
facts.easy: The Greeks took the Phoenician letters and added vowels.
facts.std: The Greeks adapted the Phoenician script and added letters for vowels, creating what is often called the first true alphabet.

facts.ja: 英語のアルファベットはラテン文字。J・U・W は、中世以降に区別されるようになった比較的新しい文字。
facts.easy: English uses the Latin alphabet. The letters J, U, and W were added quite late.
facts.std: English uses the Latin alphabet; J, U and W became distinct letters relatively late, from the Middle Ages onward.

facts.ja: 数を記録した最古級の道具の一つは、約2万年前の骨に刻み目をつけた「イシャンゴの骨」（アフリカ・コンゴで発見）。
facts.easy: One of the oldest counting tools is a bone with marks on it, from about 20,000 years ago.
facts.std: The Ishango bone, a notched bone found in Congo and dated to about 20,000 years ago, is one of the oldest known counting tools.

facts.ja: 今使われている0〜9の数字は「アラビア数字」と呼ばれるが、もとはインドで生まれ、アラビアを経てヨーロッパに広まった。
facts.easy: Our numbers 0 to 9 are called 'Arabic numerals', but they started in India.
facts.std: The digits 0–9 are called Arabic numerals but originated in India, reaching Europe through the Arab world.

facts.ja: イタリアのフィボナッチは1202年の本でインド・アラビア数字をヨーロッパに紹介した。ローマ数字より計算がずっと楽だった。
facts.easy: In 1202, Fibonacci wrote a book that brought Arabic numerals to Europe.
facts.std: Fibonacci's 1202 book Liber Abaci introduced Hindu-Arabic numerals to Europe, making calculation far easier than with Roman numerals.

facts.ja: 負の数は古代中国の数学書『九章算術』で使われていた。ヨーロッパでは長い間「ありえない数」と考えられた。
facts.easy: Negative numbers were used in ancient China. In Europe, people did not accept them for a long time.
facts.std: Negative numbers appear in the ancient Chinese text The Nine Chapters on the Mathematical Art, while European mathematicians resisted them for centuries.

facts.ja: 等号「＝」は1557年にイギリスのロバート・レコードが考えた。「2本の平行線ほど等しいものはない」からだという。
facts.easy: The equals sign '=' was invented in 1557 by Robert Recorde.
facts.std: The equals sign was introduced by Welsh mathematician Robert Recorde in 1557, who chose two parallel lines because 'no two things can be more equal'.

facts.ja: 1488年、ポルトガルのディアスがアフリカ南端の喜望峰を回った。
facts.easy: In 1488, Bartolomeu Dias sailed around the southern tip of Africa.
facts.std: In 1488 the Portuguese explorer Bartolomeu Dias rounded the Cape of Good Hope at Africa's southern tip.

facts.ja: 1492年、コロンブスは西回りでアジアを目指してカリブ海の島に着いた。本人は最後までアジアの近くだと考えていたとされる。
facts.easy: In 1492, Columbus reached islands in the Caribbean. He thought he was near Asia.
facts.std: In 1492 Columbus reached the Caribbean while seeking a western route to Asia, and reportedly believed to the end that he had reached Asia's edge.

facts.ja: 1498年、ヴァスコ・ダ・ガマがインドに到達し、ヨーロッパからアフリカを回ってアジアへ行く航路が開かれた。
facts.easy: In 1498, Vasco da Gama reached India by sailing around Africa.
facts.std: In 1498 Vasco da Gama reached India, opening a sea route from Europe to Asia around Africa.

facts.ja: マゼランの船団は1519年に出発し、1522年に初の世界一周を果たした。マゼラン本人は途中のフィリピンで戦死した。
facts.easy: Magellan's ships were the first to sail around the world, from 1519 to 1522. Magellan himself died on the way.
facts.std: Magellan's expedition, which set out in 1519, completed the first circumnavigation in 1522, though Magellan himself was killed in the Philippines.

facts.ja: 1543年、ポルトガル人を乗せた船が種子島に着き、日本に鉄砲が伝わった。
facts.easy: In 1543, Portuguese people arrived at Tanegashima and brought guns to Japan.
facts.std: In 1543 a ship carrying Portuguese traders landed on Tanegashima, introducing firearms to Japan.

facts.ja: 水深200mより深い「深海」は、地球の表面のおよそ3分の2を占めている。
facts.easy: The deep sea, below 200 meters, covers about two-thirds of Earth's surface.
facts.std: The deep sea, generally defined as below 200 meters, covers about two-thirds of Earth's surface.

facts.ja: 深海の水圧はとても高い。水深約1万mでは、指先ほどの面積に1トン以上の重さがかかるのと同じ。
facts.easy: The deep sea has very strong water pressure. At 10,000 meters, it is like one ton on your fingertip.
facts.std: Pressure in the deepest ocean exceeds 1,000 times that at the surface—more than a tonne on every square centimeter.

facts.ja: ダイオウイカが生きた姿で初めて撮影されたのは2004年で、日本の研究者による。
facts.easy: A living giant squid was first photographed in 2004 by Japanese scientists.
facts.std: The first photographs of a live giant squid in its natural habitat were taken in 2004 by Japanese researchers.

facts.ja: 深海の熱水噴出孔のまわりでは、太陽の光に頼らず、化学物質からエネルギーを得る生き物の生態系がある。
facts.easy: Near hot vents in the deep sea, living things get energy from chemicals, not sunlight.
facts.std: Around deep-sea hydrothermal vents, entire ecosystems rely on chemosynthesis rather than sunlight for energy.

facts.ja: 海底は、月の表面よりも詳しい地図が作られていないと言われる。
facts.easy: We have better maps of the Moon than of the bottom of our oceans.
facts.std: Much of the ocean floor has been mapped in less detail than the surface of the Moon.

facts.ja: エビングハウスの研究では、覚えた内容は最初の1日で急速に忘れられる。「忘却曲線」と呼ばれる。
facts.easy: We forget new things very quickly, especially on the first day. This is the 'forgetting curve'.
facts.std: Hermann Ebbinghaus showed that newly learned material is forgotten rapidly at first, especially within the first day: the 'forgetting curve'.

facts.ja: 間隔をあけて繰り返し復習すると、一度にまとめて覚えるより長く記憶に残る。「分散学習」の効果。
facts.easy: Studying a little at a time, with breaks between, helps you remember longer.
facts.std: Spacing out review sessions over time leads to longer-lasting memory than cramming, a finding known as the spacing effect.

facts.ja: 人が一度に覚えておける項目の数は、かつて「7±2」と言われたが、今は4つ前後とする研究が多い。
facts.easy: People can hold only a few things in mind at once, maybe about four.
facts.std: Working memory was once said to hold 'seven plus or minus two' items, but more recent research suggests about four.

facts.ja: 「記憶の宮殿」は、覚えたいものをよく知っている場所に置いていくように想像する記憶術。古代ギリシャから伝わる。
facts.easy: The 'memory palace' is a trick: you imagine putting things in places you know well.
facts.std: The 'memory palace', or method of loci, places items to be remembered along an imagined familiar route, a technique dating back to ancient Greece.

facts.ja: 人に教えるつもりで学ぶと、よりよく理解し覚えられるという研究がある。「教えることによる学習」と呼ばれる。
facts.easy: If you study as if you will teach it, you remember it better.
facts.std: Studies suggest that learning with the expectation of teaching others improves understanding and recall, a phenomenon called learning by teaching.

facts.ja: インターネットの前身ARPANETは、1969年にアメリカの4つの大学・研究所のコンピューターをつないで始まった。
facts.easy: ARPANET, the start of the internet, began in 1969 by connecting four computers in the US.
facts.std: ARPANET, the forerunner of the internet, began in 1969 by linking computers at four American universities and research institutes.

series.title: インターネットの歴史

facts.ja: ネットワークを通じたメールで「@」を使ったのは、1971年のレイ・トムリンソンが最初。
facts.easy: In 1971, Ray Tomlinson sent the first network email using the '@' sign.
facts.std: Ray Tomlinson sent the first networked email in 1971 and chose the @ sign to separate user and computer names.

series.title: インターネットの歴史

facts.ja: ワールド・ワイド・ウェブは、1989年にスイスのCERNでティム・バーナーズ＝リーが提案した。
facts.easy: The World Wide Web was invented in 1989 by Tim Berners-Lee in Switzerland.
facts.std: Tim Berners-Lee proposed the World Wide Web in 1989 while working at CERN in Switzerland.

series.title: インターネットの歴史

facts.ja: 誰でも編集できる百科事典ウィキペディアは2001年に始まった。
facts.easy: Wikipedia, the free encyclopedia anyone can edit, started in 2001.
facts.std: Wikipedia, the free online encyclopedia that anyone can edit, was launched in 2001.

series.title: インターネットの歴史

facts.ja: 世界の人口のおよそ3分の2がインターネットを使っている（2020年代前半の推計）。
facts.easy: About two-thirds of people in the world use the internet.
facts.std: Around two-thirds of the world's population uses the internet, according to estimates from the early 2020s.

series.title: インターネットの歴史

facts.ja: ナイル川の流域は、アフリカの11か国にまたがっている。
facts.easy: The Nile River's area covers 11 countries in Africa.
facts.std: The Nile's drainage basin spans eleven African countries.

facts.ja: アマゾン川が海に流す水の量は世界最大で、世界の川から海に流れ込む水の約5分の1を占める。
facts.easy: The Amazon carries more water than any other river. It is about one-fifth of all river water going into the sea.
facts.std: The Amazon discharges more water than any other river—about a fifth of all river water entering the oceans.

facts.ja: 長江（揚子江）はアジアで最も長い川で、全長約6300km。世界最大級の三峡ダムがある。
facts.easy: The Yangtze is the longest river in Asia. It has one of the biggest dams in the world.
facts.std: The Yangtze, about 6,300 kilometers long, is Asia's longest river and home to the Three Gorges Dam.

facts.ja: ドナウ川は10か国を流れ、世界で最も多くの国を通る川とされる。
facts.easy: The Danube River flows through 10 countries, more than any other river.
facts.std: The Danube flows through ten countries, more than any other river in the world.

facts.ja: 日本で最も長い川は信濃川で約367km。世界の大河と比べると短く、急な流れが多いのが日本の川の特徴。
facts.easy: Japan's longest river is the Shinano, about 367 km. Japanese rivers are short and fast.
facts.std: Japan's longest river, the Shinano, is about 367 kilometers long; Japanese rivers are typically short and steep.

facts.ja: 知られている最古級の楽器は、約4万年前の鳥の骨やマンモスの牙で作られた笛。ドイツの洞窟で見つかった。
facts.easy: Some of the oldest instruments are flutes made from bird bones about 40,000 years ago.
facts.std: Some of the oldest known musical instruments are flutes made from bird bone and mammoth ivory about 40,000 years ago, found in caves in Germany.

facts.ja: バイオリンは16世紀のイタリアで、今とほぼ同じ形になった。
facts.easy: The violin got its modern shape in Italy in the 1500s.
facts.std: The violin took on essentially its modern form in 16th-century Italy.

facts.ja: ピアノは1700年ごろ、イタリアのクリストフォリが発明した。
facts.easy: The piano was invented around 1700 by Cristofori in Italy.
facts.std: The piano was invented around 1700 by Bartolomeo Cristofori in Florence.

facts.ja: サクソフォンは、1840年代にベルギーのアドルフ・サックスが発明した。名前は発明者の名字から。
facts.easy: The saxophone was invented in the 1840s by Adolphe Sax. It is named after him.
facts.std: The saxophone was invented in the 1840s by the Belgian Adolphe Sax, who gave it his name.

facts.ja: エレキギターは1930年代に登場した。大きな楽団の中でギターの音が聞こえるようにするのが目的だった。
facts.easy: Electric guitars appeared in the 1930s so guitar players could be heard in big bands.
facts.std: Electric guitars emerged in the 1930s, largely so guitarists could be heard over big bands.

facts.ja: 虹は、太陽を背にしたときにしか見えない。空中の水滴が太陽の光を反射・屈折させて見える。
facts.easy: You can only see a rainbow when the sun is behind you.
facts.std: A rainbow appears only when the Sun is behind you, as sunlight is refracted and reflected by water droplets in front of you.

facts.ja: オーロラは、太陽から来た電気を帯びた粒子が地球の大気とぶつかって光る現象。
facts.easy: Auroras happen when tiny particles from the sun hit the air around Earth.
facts.std: Auroras occur when charged particles from the Sun collide with gases in Earth's upper atmosphere and make them glow.

facts.ja: 雪の結晶は基本的に六角形。水の分子が結びつくときの角度がもとになっている。
facts.easy: Snowflakes usually have six sides because of how water molecules join.
