facts.std: The Dojima Rice Exchange in Osaka, which traded contracts on future rice in the 18th century, is often described as one of the world's first organized futures markets.

facts.ja: 株価が上がる相場を「ブル（雄牛）」、下がる相場を「ベア（熊）」と呼ぶ。雄牛は角を突き上げ、熊は前足を振り下ろして攻撃することに由来するという説がある。
facts.easy: A rising market is called a 'bull' market, and a falling one is a 'bear' market.
facts.std: Rising markets are called 'bull' markets and falling ones 'bear' markets; one popular explanation is that a bull thrusts its horns up while a bear swipes its paws down.

facts.ja: 世界初の汎用クレジットカードとされるダイナースクラブカードは、1950年にアメリカで生まれた。財布を忘れて食事代を払えなかった体験がきっかけと伝えられる。
facts.easy: The Diners Club card, started in 1950, is called the first general credit card. The idea came after a man forgot his wallet at dinner.
facts.std: The Diners Club card, launched in 1950, is often called the first general-purpose charge card; its founder reportedly got the idea after forgetting his wallet at a restaurant.

facts.ja: Google の名前は、10の100乗を表す数学用語「googol」のつづりを変えたもの。膨大な情報を整理するという目標を表している。
facts.easy: The name Google comes from 'googol', a very large number: 1 followed by 100 zeros.
facts.std: Google's name is a play on 'googol', the number 1 followed by 100 zeros, reflecting its aim to organize a huge amount of information.

facts.ja: ニンテンドーは1889年に京都で花札を作る会社として始まった。ゲーム機を作るようになったのは、それから80年以上後のこと。
facts.easy: Nintendo started in 1889 in Kyoto as a company that made playing cards.
facts.std: Nintendo was founded in Kyoto in 1889 as a maker of hanafuda playing cards, decades before it entered the video game business.

facts.ja: Amazon は1994年に創業し、最初はインターネットで本だけを売る会社だった。
facts.easy: Amazon started in 1994. At first, it only sold books on the internet.
facts.std: Amazon was founded in 1994 and began as an online bookstore before expanding into almost every kind of product.

facts.ja: 1929年10月のニューヨーク株式市場の大暴落は、世界恐慌の始まりとされる。アメリカの失業率は1933年に約25％に達した。
facts.easy: The stock market crash of 1929 helped start the Great Depression. By 1933, about one in four American workers had no job.
facts.std: The Wall Street Crash of October 1929 marked the beginning of the Great Depression; US unemployment reached about 25 percent by 1933.

facts.ja: 1630年代のオランダでは、チューリップの球根の値段が異常に高くなった。「チューリップ・バブル」は歴史上の投機熱の例としてよく語られる。
facts.easy: In the 1630s in the Netherlands, tulip bulbs became very expensive. This is often called the first big price bubble.
facts.std: In the 1630s, prices for tulip bulbs in the Dutch Republic soared and then collapsed; 'tulip mania' is often cited as an early example of a speculative bubble.

facts.ja: 日本初のコンビニの一つとされるセブン-イレブンの1号店は、1974年に東京・豊洲に開店した。
facts.easy: The first 7-Eleven store in Japan opened in Toyosu, Tokyo, in 1974.
facts.std: Japan's first 7-Eleven store opened in Toyosu, Tokyo, in 1974, helping to launch the country's convenience store culture.

facts.ja: 「パレートの法則（80対20の法則）」は、結果の約8割が原因の約2割から生まれるという経験則。イタリアの経済学者パレートの観察にちなむ。
facts.easy: The 80/20 rule says that about 80% of results often come from about 20% of causes.
facts.std: The Pareto principle, or 80/20 rule, observes that roughly 80 percent of effects often come from 20 percent of causes; it is named after the economist Vilfredo Pareto.

facts.ja: トヨタの「かんばん方式」は、必要なものを必要なときに必要なだけ作る仕組み。スーパーマーケットの品出しの仕方から着想を得たと言われる。
facts.easy: Toyota's 'kanban' system makes only what is needed, when it is needed. The idea came partly from how supermarkets fill shelves.
facts.std: Toyota's kanban system, part of just-in-time production, was reportedly inspired by the way American supermarkets restocked shelves only as items were sold.

facts.ja: 複式簿記を初めて本で詳しく紹介したのは、1494年のイタリアの数学者ルカ・パチョーリ。今も会計の基本になっている。
facts.easy: In 1494, an Italian named Luca Pacioli wrote about double-entry bookkeeping. Accountants still use this method today.
facts.std: Luca Pacioli's 1494 book was the first printed work to describe double-entry bookkeeping in detail, the system still at the heart of accounting.

facts.ja: 世界最古の硬貨の一つは、紀元前600年ごろに今のトルコにあったリディア王国で作られた。金と銀の混ざった「エレクトラム」でできていた。
facts.easy: Some of the first coins were made around 600 BC in Lydia, in what is now Turkey.
facts.std: Some of the earliest known coins were minted around 600 BC in the kingdom of Lydia, in modern Turkey, from electrum, a natural mix of gold and silver.

facts.ja: 世界最古の紙幣は、11世紀の中国（宋）で使われた「交子」とされる。
facts.easy: The first paper money was used in China about 1,000 years ago.
facts.std: The first government-issued paper money, the jiaozi, appeared in Song dynasty China in the 11th century.

facts.ja: 現存する世界最古の銀行は、1472年創業のイタリアのモンテ・デイ・パスキ・ディ・シエナとされる。
facts.easy: The oldest bank still working today is in Siena, Italy. It started in 1472.
facts.std: Banca Monte dei Paschi di Siena, founded in 1472, is generally considered the oldest bank still in operation.

facts.ja: GDP（国内総生産）は、一定期間に国内で生み出された財とサービスの付加価値の合計。今のような考え方は1930年代にアメリカで整えられた。
facts.easy: GDP is the total value of goods and services a country makes in a year. The idea was developed in the 1930s.
facts.std: Gross domestic product measures the total value added by goods and services produced in a country over a period; the modern concept was developed in the 1930s.

facts.ja: ジンバブエでは2000年代後半に物価が極端に上がり、2008年には100兆ジンバブエ・ドル紙幣が発行された。
facts.easy: In 2008, prices in Zimbabwe rose so fast that the country printed a 100 trillion dollar bill.
facts.std: During Zimbabwe's hyperinflation in the late 2000s, the central bank issued a 100-trillion-dollar banknote in 2008.

facts.ja: そろばんは日本では室町時代ごろに中国から伝わったとされ、江戸時代には寺子屋で「読み・書き・そろばん」として広く教えられた。
facts.easy: The abacus came to Japan from China long ago. In the Edo period, children learned reading, writing, and the abacus.
facts.std: The abacus is thought to have reached Japan from China around the 15th or 16th century, and in the Edo period it was widely taught alongside reading and writing.

facts.ja: ショッピングカートは1937年にアメリカのスーパーの経営者シルヴァン・ゴールドマンが考えた。客が多くの品物を買えるようにするためだった。
facts.easy: The shopping cart was invented in 1937 by a supermarket owner in the US. He wanted customers to buy more.
facts.std: The shopping cart was invented in 1937 by Sylvan Goldman, an Oklahoma supermarket owner who wanted customers to be able to carry more goods.

facts.ja: バーコード（UPC）で初めて読み取られた商品は、1974年にアメリカのスーパーで売られたチューインガムだった。
facts.easy: The first product scanned with a barcode was a pack of chewing gum in 1974.
facts.std: The first product sold using a UPC barcode scan was a pack of Wrigley's chewing gum, in an Ohio supermarket in 1974.

facts.ja: セブン-イレブンの名前は、もともと朝7時から夜11時まで営業していたことから。
facts.easy: 7-Eleven got its name because stores were open from 7 am to 11 pm.
facts.std: 7-Eleven took its name from its original opening hours, 7 a.m. to 11 p.m.

facts.ja: 「スパム」（迷惑メール）の名前は、缶詰肉スパムを連呼するイギリスのコメディ番組の場面から来ている。
facts.easy: Junk email is called 'spam' because of a funny TV sketch where people keep saying 'Spam'.
facts.std: Unwanted email is called 'spam' after a Monty Python sketch in which the name of the canned meat is repeated over and over.

facts.ja: ロンドンの保険市場ロイズは、17世紀にエドワード・ロイドが開いたコーヒーハウスで、船主や商人が集まったことから始まった。
facts.easy: Lloyd's of London, a famous insurance market, began in a coffee house in the 1680s.
facts.std: Lloyd's of London grew out of Edward Lloyd's coffee house in the late 17th century, where ship owners and merchants met to arrange insurance.

facts.ja: ニューヨーク証券取引所の始まりは、1792年に24人の株式仲買人がウォール街のスズカケノキの下で結んだ「ボタンウッド協定」とされる。
facts.easy: The New York Stock Exchange began in 1792 when 24 traders made an agreement under a tree on Wall Street.
facts.std: The New York Stock Exchange traces its origins to the 1792 Buttonwood Agreement, signed by 24 brokers under a buttonwood tree on Wall Street.

facts.ja: ウォール街の名前は、17世紀にオランダ人がそこに築いた木の壁（wall）に由来する。
facts.easy: Wall Street got its name from a wooden wall that was built there in the 1600s.
facts.std: Wall Street is named after a wooden wall that Dutch settlers built along its route in the 17th century.

facts.ja: 世界で初めてフランチャイズ方式を大規模に広げた例の一つは、19世紀のシンガーミシンの販売網とされる。
facts.easy: One of the first big franchise systems was used to sell Singer sewing machines in the 1800s.
facts.std: The Singer sewing machine company is often credited with one of the first large-scale franchise systems in the 19th century.

facts.ja: アメリカで週40時間労働を早くから取り入れた企業の一つがフォード。1926年に週5日・40時間制を導入した。
facts.easy: In 1926, Ford was one of the first companies to give workers a five-day, 40-hour week.
facts.std: In 1926, the Ford Motor Company became one of the first major employers to adopt a five-day, 40-hour work week.

facts.ja: フォードは1913年に移動式の組み立てラインを導入し、T型フォード1台を作る時間を約12時間から約1時間半に縮めた。
facts.easy: In 1913, Ford started using a moving assembly line. A car could be made in about 90 minutes instead of 12 hours.
facts.std: Ford's moving assembly line, introduced in 1913, cut the time to build a Model T from about 12 hours to roughly an hour and a half.

facts.ja: 目標の立て方「SMART」は、具体的・測定できる・達成できる・関連がある・期限がある、の頭文字。1981年の論文で紹介された。
facts.easy: SMART goals are Specific, Measurable, Achievable, Relevant, and Time-bound.
facts.std: The SMART framework for goals—Specific, Measurable, Achievable, Relevant, Time-bound—was introduced in a 1981 management article.

facts.ja: PDCA（計画・実行・評価・改善）は、品質管理で知られるデミングが日本で広めた考え方がもとになっている。
facts.easy: PDCA means Plan, Do, Check, Act. It is a cycle for making work better step by step.
facts.std: The PDCA cycle—Plan, Do, Check, Act—is associated with W. Edwards Deming, whose quality-control ideas were highly influential in postwar Japan.

facts.ja: 「カイゼン（改善）」は英語にもなった日本語。現場で少しずつ改良を重ねる考え方として、世界の工場で使われている。
facts.easy: 'Kaizen' is a Japanese word used in English. It means making small improvements all the time.
facts.std: 'Kaizen', the Japanese term for continuous improvement through small changes, has been adopted in English and in factories worldwide.

facts.ja: 3M のポスト・イットは、強力な接着剤を作ろうとして失敗した「弱い接着剤」から生まれた。
facts.easy: Post-it Notes came from a failed try at making a very strong glue.
facts.std: Post-it Notes grew out of a 3M scientist's failed attempt to make a super-strong adhesive, which instead produced a weak, reusable one.

facts.ja: マクドナルドは、1940年にアメリカでマクドナルド兄弟が開いた1軒の店から始まった。
facts.easy: McDonald's started in 1940 as one restaurant run by two brothers in the US.
facts.std: McDonald's began in 1940 as a single restaurant opened by brothers Richard and Maurice McDonald in California.

facts.ja: ナイキの社名は、ギリシャ神話の勝利の女神ニケ（Nike）から取られた。
facts.easy: Nike is named after the Greek goddess of victory.
facts.std: Nike takes its name from Nike, the winged goddess of victory in Greek mythology.

facts.ja: 「ピザ2枚ルール」はアマゾンで知られる考え方で、チームはピザ2枚で足りる人数に抑えるのがよいとする。
facts.easy: Amazon's 'two-pizza rule' says a team should be small enough to share two pizzas.
facts.std: Amazon's 'two-pizza team' rule holds that a team should be small enough to be fed by two pizzas, keeping communication simple.

facts.ja: 「ブレインストーミング」は、アメリカの広告会社の経営者アレックス・オズボーンが1940〜50年代に広めた会議の方法。
facts.easy: Brainstorming was made popular by an advertising executive, Alex Osborn, in the 1940s and 1950s.
facts.std: Brainstorming as a group technique was popularized by advertising executive Alex Osborn in the 1940s and 1950s.

facts.ja: 「CEO（最高経営責任者）」という肩書きがアメリカで広く使われるようになったのは、主に1970年代以降。
facts.easy: The title 'CEO' became common in American companies mainly after the 1970s.
facts.std: The title 'chief executive officer' became widespread in American corporations largely from the 1970s onward.

facts.ja: 握手の習慣は古代から見られ、武器を持っていないことを示すためという説がよく知られている。
facts.easy: People have shaken hands for thousands of years. One idea is that it showed you had no weapon.
facts.std: Handshakes date back to ancient times; a popular theory says they began as a way to show that one's hand held no weapon.

facts.ja: ペーパークリップの今の形「ジェム型」は、19世紀末のイギリスのジェム社が売り出したとされ、特許を取った人ははっきりしていない。
facts.easy: The common paper clip shape is called the 'Gem' clip. It came from Britain in the late 1800s.
facts.std: The familiar double-loop paper clip, known as the Gem clip, appeared in Britain in the late 19th century, and its original inventor is uncertain.

facts.ja: ファクスの原理は1843年にスコットランドの時計職人アレクサンダー・ベインが特許を取っており、電話（1876年）より古い。
facts.easy: The idea of the fax machine is older than the telephone. It was patented in 1843.
facts.std: The basic principle of the fax machine was patented by Scottish inventor Alexander Bain in 1843, decades before the telephone.

facts.ja: 日経平均株価は1989年12月29日に3万8915円の最高値をつけた後、大きく下がり、この値を超えたのは2024年2月だった。
facts.easy: The Nikkei stock average hit a record at the end of 1989. It took until 2024 to go higher.
facts.std: Japan's Nikkei 225 peaked at 38,915 on December 29, 1989, and did not surpass that level again until February 2024.

facts.ja: 世界貿易機関（WTO）は1995年に発足した。前身は1947年に結ばれた関税と貿易に関する一般協定（GATT）。
facts.easy: The World Trade Organization began in 1995. Before that, there was an agreement called GATT from 1947.
facts.std: The World Trade Organization was established in 1995, succeeding the General Agreement on Tariffs and Trade, signed in 1947.

facts.ja: ユーロの紙幣と硬貨は2002年1月1日に使われ始めた。帳簿上の通貨としては1999年から存在していた。
facts.easy: Euro notes and coins were first used on January 1, 2002.
facts.std: Euro banknotes and coins entered circulation on January 1, 2002, although the euro had existed as an accounting currency since 1999.

facts.ja: 世界初の現金自動預け払い機（ATM）の一つは、1967年にロンドンの銀行に設置された。
facts.easy: One of the first cash machines (ATMs) opened in London in 1967.
facts.std: One of the world's first cash machines was installed at a Barclays branch in London in 1967.

facts.ja: 「タイム・イズ・マネー（時は金なり）」は、ベンジャミン・フランクリンが1748年の文章で書いた言葉として知られる。
facts.easy: The saying 'Time is money' is known from Benjamin Franklin's writing in 1748.
facts.std: The phrase 'Time is money' is famously associated with Benjamin Franklin, who used it in his 1748 essay 'Advice to a Young Tradesman'.

facts.ja: 日本では年末に、職場の仲間などと「忘年会」を開き、その年の苦労を忘れる習慣がある。
facts.easy: In Japan, coworkers often have a party at the end of the year to forget the year's troubles.
facts.std: In Japan, colleagues hold bōnenkai, 'forget-the-year' parties, in December to leave the year's troubles behind.

facts.ja: 「ブロックチェーン」の考え方を広く知らしめたのは、2008年に「サトシ・ナカモト」という名前で発表されたビットコインの論文。正体は今もわかっていない。
facts.easy: Bitcoin was described in 2008 by someone called 'Satoshi Nakamoto'. Nobody knows for sure who that is.
facts.std: Bitcoin was introduced in a 2008 paper by the pseudonymous 'Satoshi Nakamoto', whose real identity remains unknown.

facts.ja: 自動販売機の歴史は古く、紀元1世紀のアレクサンドリアのヘロンが、硬貨を入れると聖水が出る装置を記録している。
facts.easy: About 2,000 years ago, a man named Heron described a machine that gave holy water when you put in a coin.
facts.std: The earliest known vending machine was described by Hero of Alexandria in the first century: a coin dropped in released a measure of holy water.

facts.ja: 「ウォール・ストリート・ジャーナル」は1889年創刊。株価指数のダウ平均を考えたチャールズ・ダウが創刊者の一人。
facts.easy: The Wall Street Journal started in 1889. One of its founders, Charles Dow, also created the Dow stock index.
facts.std: The Wall Street Journal was first published in 1889; one of its founders, Charles Dow, also created the Dow Jones Industrial Average.

facts.ja: ダウ平均株価に最初に採用された銘柄のうち、長く残ったのはゼネラル・エレクトリックだったが、2018年に外された。
facts.easy: General Electric was in the Dow index for over 100 years, until 2018.
facts.std: General Electric was the last of the original Dow Jones Industrial Average companies to remain in the index, until it was removed in 2018.

facts.ja: 行動経済学の研究で、ダニエル・カーネマンは2002年、リチャード・セイラーは2017年にノーベル経済学賞を受けた。
facts.easy: Two scientists who studied how people really make money decisions won Nobel Prizes, in 2002 and 2017.
facts.std: Pioneers of behavioral economics won Nobel Prizes: Daniel Kahneman in 2002 and Richard Thaler in 2017.

facts.ja: 「損失回避」：人は同じ額でも、得をする喜びより損をする痛みを約2倍強く感じる傾向があるとされる。
facts.easy: People often feel the pain of losing money about twice as strongly as the joy of winning the same amount.
facts.std: Loss aversion describes how people tend to feel losses roughly twice as strongly as gains of the same size.

facts.ja: 「アンカリング効果」：最初に見た数字が、その後の判断に強く影響する。値引き前の価格が書いてあると安く感じるのもこのため。
facts.easy: The first number we see affects our later choices. This is called the anchoring effect.
facts.std: The anchoring effect means the first number we encounter strongly influences later judgments, which is why a crossed-out 'original price' makes a sale price look cheap.

facts.ja: ジャムの試食実験では、24種類並べたときより6種類のときのほうが、実際に買う人の割合がずっと高かった。選択肢が多すぎると選べなくなる例として知られる。
facts.easy: In one study, more people bought jam when there were 6 kinds than when there were 24 kinds.
facts.std: In a well-known study, shoppers offered 6 jams were far more likely to buy than those offered 24, an example of 'choice overload'.

facts.ja: 「サンクコスト（埋没費用）」は、もう取り戻せない費用のこと。それにこだわって損を続けてしまうことを「サンクコストの誤り」と呼ぶ。
facts.easy: A 'sunk cost' is money you already spent and cannot get back. Good decisions should not depend on it.
facts.std: A sunk cost is money already spent that cannot be recovered; continuing a failing project because of it is known as the sunk cost fallacy.

facts.ja: アダム・スミスの『国富論』は1776年に出版された。分業によってピン工場の生産量が大きく増える例が有名。
facts.easy: Adam Smith's famous book 'The Wealth of Nations' came out in 1776.
facts.std: Adam Smith's 'The Wealth of Nations', published in 1776, famously used a pin factory to show how the division of labor raises productivity.

facts.ja: 「見えざる手」はアダム・スミスの言葉として有名だが、『国富論』の中でこの表現が出てくるのは1回だけ。
facts.easy: Adam Smith's phrase 'invisible hand' is very famous, but it appears only once in 'The Wealth of Nations'.
facts.std: Although 'the invisible hand' is closely associated with Adam Smith, the phrase appears only once in 'The Wealth of Nations'.

facts.ja: 『エコノミスト』誌のビッグマック指数は、各国のビッグマックの値段を比べて通貨の割安・割高を見る指標。1986年に始まった。
facts.easy: The Big Mac Index compares the price of a Big Mac in different countries to see if money is cheap or expensive.
facts.std: The Economist's Big Mac Index, launched in 1986, compares burger prices across countries as a light-hearted guide to whether currencies are over- or undervalued.

facts.ja: 規格化された輸送用コンテナは1950年代にアメリカのマルコム・マクリーンが広め、船の積み下ろしの費用を大きく下げた。
facts.easy: Shipping containers became common in the 1950s. They made moving goods by ship much cheaper.
facts.std: Standardized shipping containers, popularized by Malcom McLean in the 1950s, dramatically reduced the cost of loading and unloading ships.

facts.ja: 世界の貿易品の約8割（量で見て）は船で運ばれている。
facts.easy: About 80% of world trade goods travel by ship.
facts.std: By volume, around 80 percent of global trade is carried by sea.

facts.ja: スエズ運河は1869年に開通し、ヨーロッパとアジアの船の航路を大きく短くした。
facts.easy: The Suez Canal opened in 1869. Ships between Europe and Asia no longer had to go around Africa.
facts.std: The Suez Canal, opened in 1869, allowed ships to travel between Europe and Asia without sailing around Africa.

facts.ja: 日本の消費税は1989年に3％で始まり、1997年に5％、2014年に8％、2019年に10％（食料品などは8％）になった。
facts.easy: Japan's consumption tax started at 3% in 1989. Since 2019, it has been 10%.
facts.std: Japan introduced a 3 percent consumption tax in 1989, raising it to 5 percent in 1997, 8 percent in 2014 and 10 percent in 2019, with a reduced rate for food.

facts.ja: 日本の一万円札の肖像は、2024年に福沢諭吉から「日本資本主義の父」と呼ばれる渋沢栄一に変わった。
facts.easy: Since 2024, Japan's 10,000 yen note shows Shibusawa Eiichi, who started about 500 companies.
facts.std: In 2024, Japan's 10,000-yen note switched its portrait to Shibusawa Eiichi, often called the father of Japanese capitalism for helping found hundreds of companies.

facts.ja: 日本銀行は1882年に設立された。
facts.easy: The Bank of Japan was started in 1882.
facts.std: The Bank of Japan, the country's central bank, was established in 1882.

facts.ja: アメリカの中央銀行制度（FRB）は1913年に作られた。それまでアメリカには長く中央銀行がなかった。
facts.easy: The US central bank system, the Federal Reserve, started in 1913.
facts.std: The Federal Reserve System, the central bank of the United States, was created in 1913.

facts.ja: 日本銀行は2016年に一部の預金の金利をマイナスにした。お金を預けると手数料を取られるような状態で、2024年に終わった。
facts.easy: In 2016, the Bank of Japan started 'negative interest rates'. This ended in 2024.
facts.std: The Bank of Japan introduced a negative interest rate on some bank reserves in 2016 and ended the policy in 2024.

facts.ja: 国際通貨基金（IMF）と世界銀行は、1944年のブレトン・ウッズ会議で設立が決まった。
facts.easy: The IMF and the World Bank were planned at a meeting in Bretton Woods, USA, in 1944.
facts.std: The International Monetary Fund and the World Bank were both created at the Bretton Woods Conference in 1944.

facts.ja: 戦後の日本では1949年から1971年まで、1ドル＝360円の固定相場だった。
facts.easy: From 1949 to 1971, one US dollar was always 360 yen.
facts.std: From 1949 until 1971, the yen was fixed at 360 to the US dollar under the Bretton Woods system.

facts.ja: アップルは1976年に、スティーブ・ジョブズとスティーブ・ウォズニアックらがガレージで始めたとされる。
facts.easy: Apple was started in 1976 by Steve Jobs and Steve Wozniak, famously in a garage.
facts.std: Apple was founded in 1976 by Steve Jobs, Steve Wozniak and Ronald Wayne, with early work famously done in the Jobs family garage.

facts.ja: アップルの創業者の一人ロナルド・ウェインは、創業から12日ほどで自分の持ち分を800ドルで手放した。
facts.easy: One of Apple's first founders sold his share for 800 dollars after about two weeks.
facts.std: Ronald Wayne, Apple's third co-founder, sold his 10 percent stake for 800 dollars about twelve days after the company was formed.

facts.ja: ソニーの前身「東京通信工業」は1946年に創業し、最初の製品の一つは電気炊飯器だったが、うまく売れなかった。
facts.easy: Sony started in 1946. One of its first products was a rice cooker, but it did not sell well.
facts.std: Sony began in 1946 as Tokyo Tsushin Kogyo; one of its first products was an electric rice cooker that failed commercially.

facts.ja: トヨタグループの始まりは豊田佐吉の自動織機。自動車部門は織機会社の一部門として始まった。
facts.easy: Toyota began as a company that made weaving machines.
facts.std: The Toyota group began with Sakichi Toyoda's automatic looms; car-making started as a division of the loom company.

facts.ja: ホンダが最初に売った製品は、自転車に取り付ける小さなエンジンだった。
facts.easy: Honda's first product was a small engine for bicycles.
facts.std: Honda's first product was a small auxiliary engine that could be attached to bicycles.

facts.ja: インスタントラーメンは1958年に安藤百福が発明し、カップヌードルは1971年に発売された。
facts.easy: Instant noodles were invented in Japan in 1958. Cup Noodles came out in 1971.
facts.std: Instant noodles were invented by Momofuku Ando in 1958, and Cup Noodles followed in 1971.

facts.ja: ソニーのウォークマンは1979年に発売された。社内では「録音できないテレコは売れない」と反対の声もあった。
facts.easy: The Sony Walkman came out in 1979. Some people at Sony thought it would not sell.
facts.std: Sony launched the Walkman in 1979, despite internal doubts that a cassette player without recording would sell.

facts.ja: 初代 iPhone は2007年に発表された。
facts.easy: The first iPhone was shown to the world in 2007.
facts.std: The first iPhone was unveiled by Steve Jobs in January 2007.

facts.ja: 写真フィルムで有名だったコダックの技術者は1975年にデジタルカメラを試作したが、会社は主力のフィルム事業を優先した。コダックは2012年に経営破綻した。
facts.easy: An engineer at Kodak made a digital camera in 1975. But Kodak focused on film and went bankrupt in 2012.
facts.std: A Kodak engineer built an early digital camera in 1975, but the company stayed focused on film and filed for bankruptcy in 2012.

facts.ja: レンタルビデオのブロックバスターは、2000年に当時小さかったネットフリックスを5000万ドルで買う機会を断ったと伝えられる。
facts.easy: In 2000, the video rental company Blockbuster reportedly said no to buying Netflix for 50 million dollars.
facts.std: Blockbuster reportedly turned down a chance to buy Netflix for 50 million dollars in 2000; it later went bankrupt while Netflix grew enormously.

facts.ja: 評価額10億ドル以上の未上場のスタートアップを「ユニコーン」と呼ぶ。2013年に投資家のアイリーン・リーが名付けた。
facts.easy: A startup worth over one billion dollars is called a 'unicorn', because it is so rare.
facts.std: A privately held startup valued at over one billion dollars is called a 'unicorn', a term coined by investor Aileen Lee in 2013.

facts.ja: 「ピボット」は事業の方向を大きく変えること。写真共有の Instagram は、もとは位置情報アプリ「Burbn」だった。
facts.easy: Instagram started as a different app called Burbn. Changing direction like this is called a 'pivot'.
facts.std: A 'pivot' is a major change of business direction; Instagram, for example, began as a location check-in app called Burbn.

facts.ja: Slack は、もともとオンラインゲームを作っていたチームが社内で使っていた連絡ツールから生まれた。
facts.easy: Slack started as a chat tool used inside a team that was making a video game.
facts.std: Slack grew out of an internal chat tool used by a team developing an online game that was never commercially successful.

facts.ja: 「ピーターの法則」は、人は能力の限界のポストまで昇進していく、という皮肉な経験則。1969年の本で広まった。
facts.easy: The 'Peter Principle' says people get promoted until they reach a job they cannot do well.
facts.std: The Peter Principle, from a 1969 book, holds that people in a hierarchy tend to be promoted until they reach a level where they are no longer competent.

facts.ja: 「パーキンソンの法則」：仕事は、与えられた時間をすべて使い切るまで膨らむ。1955年の雑誌記事で紹介された。
facts.easy: Parkinson's Law says work grows to fill the time you have for it.
facts.std: Parkinson's law, first stated in a 1955 essay in The Economist, holds that work expands to fill the time available for its completion.

facts.ja: 「自転車置き場の議論」：会議では、大事で難しい議題より、誰でも意見を言いやすい小さな議題に時間がかかりがちという法則。
facts.easy: In meetings, people often spend more time on small, easy topics than on big, hard ones. This is called 'bikeshedding'.
facts.std: 'Bikeshedding', or Parkinson's law of triviality, describes how meetings spend disproportionate time on trivial issues that everyone can comment on.

facts.ja: ポモドーロ・テクニックは25分の作業と5分の休憩を繰り返す時間管理法。名前はトマト型のキッチンタイマーから。
facts.easy: The Pomodoro method means working for 25 minutes and then resting for 5. 'Pomodoro' means tomato in Italian.
facts.std: The Pomodoro Technique alternates 25 minutes of focused work with short breaks; it is named after a tomato-shaped kitchen timer.

facts.ja: アイゼンハワー・マトリクスは、仕事を「緊急か」「重要か」の2つの軸で4つに分けて優先順位を決める方法。
facts.easy: The Eisenhower Matrix puts tasks into four boxes: urgent or not, and important or not.
facts.std: The Eisenhower Matrix sorts tasks into four boxes by urgency and importance to help decide what to do first, delegate, schedule or drop.

facts.ja: 「テレワーク」という言葉は、1970年代のアメリカで石油危機のころに使われ始めた。
facts.easy: The word 'telecommuting' was first used in the 1970s in the US.
facts.std: The term 'telecommuting' was coined in the United States in the 1970s, during the oil crisis.

facts.ja: 日本の「働き方改革関連法」では、2019年から残業時間に原則月45時間・年360時間の上限が設けられた。
facts.easy: Since 2019, Japan's law limits overtime to 45 hours a month in most cases.
facts.std: Under Japan's work-style reform laws, from 2019 overtime has generally been capped at 45 hours a month and 360 hours a year.

facts.ja: フランスでは法律で年5週間の有給休暇が定められている。
facts.easy: In France, workers get five weeks of paid holiday a year by law.
facts.std: French law guarantees employees five weeks of paid annual leave.

facts.ja: アメリカには、国の法律で有給休暇を義務づける制度がない。
facts.easy: The United States has no national law that requires paid holidays for workers.
facts.std: The United States is unusual among rich countries in having no federal law requiring paid vacation.

facts.ja: 「ブランド」の語源は、家畜に押す焼き印（burn と同じ語源）。持ち主を示す印だった。
facts.easy: The word 'brand' first meant a mark burned onto animals to show who owned them.
facts.std: 'Brand' originally referred to a mark burned onto livestock to show ownership, from an old word related to 'burn'.

facts.ja: 「ペルソナ」はマーケティングで、典型的な顧客像を一人の人物として具体的に描いたもの。名前や年齢、悩みまで決める。
facts.easy: In marketing, a 'persona' is an imaginary customer with a name, age, and needs.
facts.std: In marketing, a persona is a detailed fictional profile of a typical customer, including name, age, goals and frustrations.

facts.ja: マーケティングの「4P」は、製品（Product）・価格（Price）・流通（Place）・販促（Promotion）。1960年に提唱された。
facts.easy: The '4 Ps' of marketing are Product, Price, Place, and Promotion.
facts.std: The '4 Ps' of marketing—product, price, place and promotion—were proposed by E. Jerome McCarthy in 1960.

facts.ja: 顧客満足の指標NPSは、「この会社を友人に勧めますか」を0〜10で聞くだけの質問から計算する。
facts.easy: The NPS score asks one question: 'How likely are you to recommend us to a friend?', from 0 to 10.
facts.std: The Net Promoter Score is based on a single question: how likely, on a scale of 0 to 10, a customer is to recommend the company to a friend.

facts.ja: 「A/Bテスト」は、2つの案をランダムに分けた利用者に見せて、どちらがよい結果になるかを比べる方法。
facts.easy: An A/B test shows two versions to different users and checks which one works better.
facts.std: An A/B test randomly shows two versions of something to different users to measure which performs better.

facts.ja: 商品の「ロングテール」：ネット通販では、あまり売れない多くの商品の売上を合わせると、人気商品に匹敵することがある。2004年に広まった考え方。
facts.easy: Online shops can sell many products that are not popular. Together, these can sell as much as the hits. This is the 'long tail'.
facts.std: The 'long tail' idea, popularized in 2004, says online retailers can earn as much from many niche products combined as from a few best-sellers.

facts.ja: 「フリーミアム」は、基本は無料で、高度な機能だけ有料にする商売のやり方。free（無料）と premium（割増）を合わせた言葉。
facts.easy: 'Freemium' means the basic product is free, but extra features cost money.
facts.std: 'Freemium', a blend of 'free' and 'premium', is a business model offering a basic product for free while charging for extra features.

facts.ja: 「ESG投資」は、環境（Environment）・社会（Social）・企業統治（Governance）への取り組みも見て投資先を選ぶ考え方。
facts.easy: ESG investing looks at a company's care for the environment, society, and good management.
facts.std: ESG investing considers a company's environmental, social and governance practices alongside its financial results.

facts.ja: English（英語）は、5世紀ごろイギリスに渡ったゲルマン人の一派「アングル人（Angles）」の名前から来ている。
facts.easy: The word 'English' comes from the Angles, a people who came to Britain about 1,500 years ago.
facts.std: 'English' derives from the Angles, one of the Germanic peoples who settled in Britain in the fifth century.

facts.ja: Japan は、中国語の「日本」の昔の発音がマルコ・ポーロらを通じてヨーロッパに伝わったものと考えられている。
facts.easy: The word 'Japan' probably came to Europe from an old Chinese way of saying 日本.
facts.std: 'Japan' is thought to come from an early Chinese pronunciation of 日本, which reached Europe through traders and travelers such as Marco Polo.

facts.ja: school（学校）は、ギリシャ語の scholē（暇・余暇）から。もとは「暇な時間に学問や議論をすること」を指した。
facts.easy: 'School' comes from a Greek word that meant 'free time'. People used free time to learn.
facts.std: 'School' comes from Greek scholē, meaning 'leisure', since learning and discussion were what people did with free time.

facts.ja: marathon（マラソン）は、古代ギリシャの戦いの地マラトンから。勝利を伝えるため走った兵士の伝説にちなむ。
facts.easy: 'Marathon' comes from Marathon, a place in Greece. A soldier is said to have run from there with news of a victory.
facts.std: The marathon is named after Marathon in Greece, from the legend of a messenger who ran to Athens to announce a victory.

facts.ja: salad（サラダ）も salt（塩）と同じ語源。古代ローマでは野菜に塩をふって食べたことから。
facts.easy: 'Salad' comes from the Latin word for salt. Romans put salt on vegetables.
facts.std: 'Salad' derives from Latin sal, 'salt', because Romans seasoned raw vegetables with salt.

facts.ja: Monday（月曜日）は moon の日、Sunday は sun の日。英語の曜日の名前は天体や神々に由来する。
facts.easy: Monday is the moon's day, and Sunday is the sun's day.
facts.std: Monday is literally 'moon day' and Sunday 'sun day'; the English weekday names come from heavenly bodies and gods.

facts.ja: Thursday（木曜日）は、北欧神話の雷の神トール（Thor）の日。
facts.easy: Thursday means 'Thor's day'. Thor is the god of thunder in Norse stories.
facts.std: Thursday means 'Thor's day', after the Norse god of thunder.

facts.ja: September（9月）の sept はラテン語で「7」。古代ローマの暦では1年が3月から始まり、7番目の月だった。
facts.easy: 'September' comes from the Latin word for seven. In the old Roman calendar, it was the seventh month.
facts.std: September comes from Latin septem, 'seven', because it was the seventh month in the early Roman calendar, which began in March.

facts.ja: July（7月）はユリウス・カエサル、August（8月）は初代ローマ皇帝アウグストゥスにちなむ。
facts.easy: July is named after Julius Caesar, and August after the Roman emperor Augustus.
facts.std: July is named after Julius Caesar and August after Augustus, the first Roman emperor.

facts.ja: January（1月）は、ローマ神話の門と始まりの神ヤヌスにちなむ。ヤヌスは前と後ろの2つの顔を持つ。
facts.easy: January is named after Janus, a Roman god of doors and beginnings. He has two faces.
facts.std: January is named after Janus, the two-faced Roman god of doorways and beginnings, who looks both back and forward.

facts.ja: business は busy（忙しい）＋ -ness。もとは「忙しい状態」を意味していた。
facts.easy: 'Business' comes from 'busy'. It first meant the state of being busy.
facts.std: 'Business' is simply 'busy' plus '-ness', originally meaning the state of being busy.

facts.ja: career（経歴）は、フランス語の carrière（競走路・馬車の道）から。人生を走る道というイメージ。
facts.easy: 'Career' comes from an old French word for a racecourse or road.
facts.std: 'Career' comes from French carrière, a racecourse or road, giving the image of the course one runs through life.

facts.ja: client（顧客）はラテン語の cliens から。古代ローマで有力者の保護を受ける人を指した。
facts.easy: 'Client' comes from a Latin word for a person protected by a powerful man in ancient Rome.
facts.std: 'Client' comes from Latin cliens, a person under the protection of a powerful patron in ancient Rome.

facts.ja: manager はイタリア語の maneggiare（手で扱う、馬を操る）から。ラテン語の manus（手）にさかのぼる。
facts.easy: 'Manager' comes from an Italian word meaning 'to handle', from the Latin word for hand.
facts.std: 'Manager' traces back to Italian maneggiare, 'to handle, to train horses', from Latin manus, 'hand'.

facts.ja: graduate（卒業する）は、ラテン語の gradus（段・階段）から。一段上に進むこと。
facts.easy: 'Graduate' comes from the Latin word for 'step'. You go up one step.
facts.std: 'Graduate' comes from Latin gradus, 'step', as in moving up a step in rank or learning.

facts.ja: muscle（筋肉）はラテン語の musculus（小さなネズミ）から。筋肉が動く様子が皮膚の下のネズミのように見えたためと言われる。
facts.easy: 'Muscle' comes from a Latin word meaning 'little mouse'. A moving muscle looked like a mouse under the skin.
facts.std: 'Muscle' comes from Latin musculus, 'little mouse', perhaps because a flexing muscle looks like a mouse moving under the skin.

facts.ja: window（窓）は、古ノルド語の「風（vindr）の目（auga）」から。昔の窓はガラスのない穴だった。
facts.easy: 'Window' comes from Old Norse words meaning 'wind eye'. Old windows were just holes.
facts.std: 'Window' comes from Old Norse vindauga, literally 'wind eye', from the time when windows were simply openings.

facts.ja: dandelion（タンポポ）は、フランス語の dent de lion（ライオンの歯）から。ぎざぎざの葉の形にちなむ。
facts.easy: 'Dandelion' comes from French words meaning 'lion's tooth', because of its sharp leaves.
facts.std: 'Dandelion' comes from French dent de lion, 'lion's tooth', after the jagged shape of its leaves.

facts.ja: hippopotamus（カバ）は、ギリシャ語で「川の馬」という意味。
facts.easy: 'Hippopotamus' means 'river horse' in Greek.
facts.std: 'Hippopotamus' comes from Greek words meaning 'river horse'.

facts.ja: octopus（タコ）はギリシャ語で「8本の足」。octo- は8を表し、October ももとは8番目の月だった。
facts.easy: 'Octopus' means 'eight feet' in Greek.
facts.std: 'Octopus' means 'eight-footed' in Greek; the same 'octo-' for eight appears in October, once the eighth month.

facts.ja: dinosaur（恐竜）は、ギリシャ語の「恐ろしい（deinos）トカゲ（sauros）」から。1842年に作られた言葉。
facts.easy: 'Dinosaur' means 'terrible lizard' in Greek. The word was made in 1842.
facts.std: 'Dinosaur' was coined in 1842 by Richard Owen from Greek words meaning 'terrible lizard'.

facts.ja: scientist（科学者）という言葉は、1833年にイギリスのウィリアム・ヒューウェルが作った。それまでは natural philosopher などと呼ばれていた。
facts.easy: The word 'scientist' was first used in 1833.
facts.std: The word 'scientist' was coined by William Whewell in 1833; before that, scientists were usually called natural philosophers.

facts.ja: robot（ロボット）は、1920年のチェコの劇『R.U.R.』で使われた言葉。チェコ語の robota（強制労働）から。
facts.easy: 'Robot' comes from a Czech play from 1920. It comes from a Czech word for hard work.
facts.std: 'Robot' first appeared in Karel Čapek's 1920 play R.U.R., from Czech robota, 'forced labor'.

facts.ja: jeans（ジーンズ）は、丈夫な綿布の産地だったイタリアの港町ジェノバ（フランス語で Gênes）の名前から。
facts.easy: 'Jeans' comes from Genoa, an Italian city known for strong cotton cloth.
facts.std: 'Jeans' takes its name from Genoa, the Italian port known for a sturdy cotton cloth, called Gênes in French.

facts.ja: computer は、もともと「計算する人」という職業の名前だった。
facts.easy: A 'computer' was first a person whose job was to do calculations.
facts.std: 'Computer' originally meant a person whose job was to perform calculations, before it came to mean a machine.

facts.ja: Wi-Fi は「Wireless Fidelity」の略だと思われがちだが、実はもともと特に意味のないブランド名として作られた。
facts.easy: Many people think Wi-Fi means 'wireless fidelity', but it was made as a brand name with no meaning.
facts.std: Wi-Fi is often said to stand for 'wireless fidelity', but the name was created as a catchy brand name with no specific meaning.

facts.ja: Bluetooth は、10世紀にデンマークとノルウェーを統一した王ハーラル「青歯王」のあだ名から。機器をつなぐ技術を、国をまとめた王になぞらえた。
facts.easy: Bluetooth is named after a Danish king called Harald Bluetooth, who united people. The technology connects devices.
facts.std: Bluetooth is named after Harald 'Bluetooth', a tenth-century king who united Denmark and Norway, just as the technology unites devices.

facts.ja: メールの「@」は英語で at sign。イタリア語では「カタツムリ」、オランダ語では「サルのしっぽ」などと呼ばれる。
facts.easy: In English, @ is the 'at sign'. In Italian it is called 'snail', and in Dutch 'monkey tail'.
facts.std: The @ symbol is called the 'at sign' in English, but 'snail' in Italian and 'monkey's tail' in Dutch.

facts.ja: 記号「#」は英語で hash、number sign、アメリカでは pound sign とも呼ばれる。SNSの「ハッシュタグ」の hash はここから。
facts.easy: The symbol # has many names, like 'hash' and 'pound sign'. 'Hashtag' comes from 'hash'.
facts.std: The # symbol is called a hash, number sign or, in the US, pound sign; 'hashtag' comes from 'hash'.

facts.ja: orange（オレンジ）は、もとは an norange だったが、n が冠詞に移って an orange になった。
facts.easy: 'An orange' was once 'a norange'. The 'n' moved from the word to 'an'.
facts.std: 'Orange' comes ultimately from Sanskrit via Arabic naranj; in English, 'a norange' was reanalyzed as 'an orange'.

facts.ja: adder（クサリヘビ）も、もとは a nadder だったのが an adder になった。apron（エプロン）も a napron から。
facts.easy: 'An adder' (a snake) was once 'a nadder'. 'An apron' was once 'a napron'.
facts.std: 'Adder' was originally 'nadder', and 'apron' was 'napron'; in both, the n shifted to the article 'an'.

facts.ja: calculate（計算する）は、ラテン語の calculus（小石）から。昔は小石を使って数を数えていた。
facts.easy: 'Calculate' comes from a Latin word for small stone. People used stones to count.
facts.std: 'Calculate' comes from Latin calculus, 'small pebble', because pebbles were used for counting.

facts.ja: alcohol, algebra, sugar, coffee はアラビア語から英語に入った言葉。
facts.easy: The words 'alcohol', 'algebra', 'sugar', and 'coffee' came into English from Arabic.
facts.std: Many English words, including alcohol, algebra, sugar and coffee, came from Arabic, often through other European languages.

facts.ja: algorithm（アルゴリズム）は、9世紀のペルシャの数学者アル＝フワーリズミーの名前から。
facts.easy: 'Algorithm' comes from the name of a Persian mathematician from the 800s.
facts.std: 'Algorithm' comes from the name of al-Khwarizmi, a ninth-century Persian mathematician.

facts.ja: tsunami は日本語から英語に入った言葉。英語では以前 tidal wave（潮の波）とも呼ばれたが、潮とは関係ないため tsunami が定着した。
facts.easy: 'Tsunami' is a Japanese word used in English.
facts.std: 'Tsunami' was borrowed from Japanese; it replaced 'tidal wave' in scientific use because such waves have nothing to do with tides.

facts.ja: tycoon（大物実業家）は日本語の「大君（たいくん）」から。幕末に外国人が将軍をこう呼んだ。
facts.easy: 'Tycoon', a very rich businessperson, comes from the Japanese word 'taikun'.
facts.std: 'Tycoon', meaning a powerful businessperson, comes from Japanese taikun, a title foreigners used for the shogun.

facts.ja: karaoke は「空（から）＋オーケストラ」を縮めた日本語。歌のない伴奏という意味。
facts.easy: 'Karaoke' comes from Japanese words meaning 'empty orchestra'.
facts.std: 'Karaoke' is a Japanese blend of kara, 'empty', and ōkesutora, 'orchestra': music without the singer.

facts.ja: emoji（絵文字）は日本語の「絵＋文字」。英語の emotion に似ているのは偶然。
facts.easy: 'Emoji' comes from Japanese: 'e' (picture) and 'moji' (character). It is not related to 'emotion'.
facts.std: 'Emoji' comes from Japanese e, 'picture', and moji, 'character'; its resemblance to 'emotion' is a coincidence.

facts.ja: 英語の typhoon（台風）は、中国語やアラビア語、ギリシャ語など複数の言葉の影響を受けて今の形になったとされる。
facts.easy: The word 'typhoon' came into English from several languages, including Chinese and Arabic.
facts.std: 'Typhoon' has a mixed origin, influenced by Chinese, Arabic and Greek words before settling into its English form.

facts.ja: tomato（トマト）と chocolate（チョコレート）は、メキシコのナワトル語から来た言葉。
facts.easy: The words 'tomato' and 'chocolate' come from Nahuatl, a language of Mexico.
facts.std: 'Tomato' and 'chocolate' both come from Nahuatl, the language of the Aztecs, via Spanish.

facts.ja: pajamas（パジャマ）と shampoo（シャンプー）は、インドの言葉から英語に入った。shampoo はもとは「マッサージする」という意味。
facts.easy: 'Pajamas' and 'shampoo' came into English from languages of India.
facts.std: 'Pajamas' and 'shampoo' entered English from Indian languages; 'shampoo' originally meant 'to massage'.

facts.ja: ketchup は、中国南部の言葉で魚醤を指した言葉が由来とされる。もとはトマトを使っていなかった。
facts.easy: 'Ketchup' probably came from a Chinese word for fish sauce. It did not have tomatoes at first.
facts.std: 'Ketchup' probably comes from a southern Chinese word for a fermented fish sauce; early ketchups contained no tomatoes.

facts.ja: orangutan は、マレー語で「森の人」という意味。
facts.easy: 'Orangutan' means 'person of the forest' in Malay.
facts.std: 'Orangutan' comes from Malay words meaning 'person of the forest'.

facts.ja: kangaroo は、オーストラリア先住民のグーグ・イミディル語から。「わからない」という意味だという話は俗説で、正しくない。
facts.easy: 'Kangaroo' comes from an Aboriginal language. The story that it means 'I don't know' is not true.
facts.std: 'Kangaroo' comes from the Guugu Yimithirr language of Australia; the popular story that it means 'I don't understand' is a myth.

facts.ja: 「メーデー（Mayday）」という救難信号は、フランス語の m'aider（助けて）に由来する。
facts.easy: The emergency call 'Mayday' comes from French words meaning 'help me'.
facts.std: The distress call 'Mayday' comes from French m'aider, 'help me'.

facts.ja: denim（デニム）は、フランスの町ニームの「serge de Nîmes（ニームの織物）」から。
facts.easy: 'Denim' comes from French words meaning 'cloth from Nîmes', a town in France.
facts.std: 'Denim' comes from French serge de Nîmes, a fabric from the town of Nîmes.

facts.ja: o'clock は of the clock の短縮形。「時計によれば」という意味。
facts.easy: 'O'clock' is a short form of 'of the clock'.
facts.std: 'O'clock' is a contraction of 'of the clock', meaning 'according to the clock'.

facts.ja: a.m. と p.m. はラテン語の ante meridiem（正午の前）と post meridiem（正午の後）の略。
facts.easy: 'a.m.' and 'p.m.' come from Latin words meaning 'before midday' and 'after midday'.
facts.std: 'a.m.' and 'p.m.' abbreviate Latin ante meridiem, 'before midday', and post meridiem, 'after midday'.

facts.ja: e.g. はラテン語の exempli gratia（例えば）、i.e. は id est（つまり）の略。
facts.easy: 'e.g.' means 'for example', and 'i.e.' means 'that is'. Both come from Latin.
facts.std: 'e.g.' abbreviates Latin exempli gratia, 'for example', while 'i.e.' stands for id est, 'that is'.

facts.ja: etc. はラテン語の et cetera（そしてその他のもの）の略。
facts.easy: 'etc.' comes from the Latin 'et cetera', meaning 'and the other things'.
facts.std: 'etc.' is short for Latin et cetera, 'and the rest'.
